sections.title: Designing Instruction and Assessment to Promote Student Learning
sections.summary: 20 lessons for Domain 1 (34% of the exam).

topics.title: Human Development and the Learning Process

blocks.text: Effective teachers understand that students grow along predictable yet individually variable paths across cognitive, physical, social, and emotional domains. Knowing these patterns lets a teacher set developmentally appropriate expectations and design instruction that meets learners where they are. Piaget's stages describe how thinking matures from concrete to abstract, while Vygotsky emphasizes that learning is social and occurs within the zone of proximal development when supported by a more knowledgeable other. Maslow reminds teachers that unmet basic needs interfere with learning, and Erikson highlights the psychosocial challenges students face at each age. Brain-based principles show that prior knowledge, active engagement, motivation, and meaningful practice all strengthen learning. Teachers must recognize that development in one domain affects the others, that students of the same age can differ widely, and that environment, culture, and experience shape growth. The exam expects teachers to apply these theories practically: scaffolding tasks, building on prior knowledge, fostering intrinsic motivation, and creating safe conditions for risk-taking. Understanding readiness, developmental milestones, and how memory and transfer work allows teachers to plan lessons that are challenging yet attainable for every learner.

items: Piaget describes cognitive stages; learners move from concrete to abstract thinking over time.
Vygotsky's zone of proximal development frames learning as social and supported by scaffolding.
Maslow's hierarchy: unmet basic and safety needs block engagement and higher-order learning.
Development across cognitive, physical, social, and emotional domains is interrelated.
Same-age students vary widely; instruction must match individual readiness and prior knowledge.
Intrinsic motivation, active engagement, and meaningful practice deepen retention and transfer.
Developmentally appropriate expectations prevent frustration and support continued growth.

blocks.text: Every classroom contains learners who differ in background, language, ability, interest, and readiness. Competent teachers see this diversity as an asset and adjust instruction so all students can access rigorous content. Differentiation means varying the content, process, product, or learning environment in response to student needs while maintaining high expectations for everyone. Teachers must understand cultural and linguistic diversity, the needs of English learners, gifted students, and students with disabilities, and how socioeconomic factors influence learning. Culturally responsive teaching validates students' identities, connects learning to their experiences, and avoids stereotyping or deficit thinking. Flexible grouping, tiered assignments, choice boards, varied questioning, and multiple means of representation help reach diverse learners. Teachers should use data and ongoing observation to plan responsive supports and accommodations rather than lowering standards. Knowing legal protections and the value of inclusion guides equitable practice. The exam emphasizes proactive planning—anticipating barriers and designing instruction accessible to all from the start—over reactive remediation. Effective teachers create inclusive communities where differences are respected and every student is held to challenging, attainable goals.

items: Differentiate content, process, product, or environment while keeping expectations high for all.
Culturally responsive teaching affirms identity and connects content to students' lived experiences.
Avoid deficit thinking and stereotypes; treat diversity as a classroom asset.
Support English learners with comprehensible input, visuals, and language scaffolds.
Use flexible grouping, tiered tasks, and choice to address varied readiness and interests.
Plan proactively (universal design) to remove barriers before they arise.
Provide accommodations and inclusion without diluting rigor or standards.

topics.title: Designing Instruction Aligned to the TEKS

blocks.text: Strong instruction begins with clear, measurable objectives derived from the Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS), the state's required curriculum. Teachers practice backward design: identify what students should know and do, decide how mastery will be demonstrated, and then plan learning experiences that build toward those goals. Objectives should be specific, aligned to grade-level standards, and communicated to students. Effective unit and lesson plans sequence content logically, activate prior knowledge, incorporate appropriate pacing, and include opportunities for guided and independent practice. Teachers select instructional strategies, materials, and resources that match objectives and learner needs, and they plan for higher-order thinking, not just recall. Alignment among objectives, instruction, and assessment is essential; a lesson is coherent when what is taught and tested reflects the stated goals. Teachers also plan transitions, anticipate misconceptions, and prepare relevant examples. The exam expects teachers to connect daily lessons to broader curricular goals and real-world relevance, organize content to support retention and transfer, and design engaging, standards-based learning experiences that are rigorous, purposeful, and developmentally appropriate.

items: TEKS are the required Texas standards; objectives must align to grade-level expectations.
Use backward design: define goals, then assessment evidence, then learning activities.
Write specific, measurable objectives and share them clearly with students.
Ensure tight alignment among objectives, instruction, and assessment.
Sequence content logically, activate prior knowledge, and pace appropriately.
Plan for higher-order thinking and real-world relevance, not just recall.
Anticipate misconceptions and prepare examples, transitions, and practice opportunities.

topics.title: Assessment to Guide Learning and Instruction

blocks.text: Assessment is integral to teaching, not separate from it. Teachers must understand the purposes and types of assessment and use them to inform instruction and support learning. Formative assessment occurs during learning to give feedback and adjust teaching, while summative assessment measures mastery at the end of a unit or course. Diagnostic assessment identifies prior knowledge and needs before instruction. Quality assessments are valid (measure what they intend), reliable (consistent), and free of bias. Teachers align assessments to objectives and use varied methods—observations, performance tasks, portfolios, rubrics, selected- and constructed-response items—to capture different kinds of learning. Clear criteria and rubrics make expectations transparent and feedback actionable. Teachers analyze assessment data to identify patterns, group students, reteach, and differentiate. They also involve students through self-assessment and goal-setting, which builds metacognition and ownership. Accommodations ensure fair measurement for diverse learners. The exam emphasizes using assessment results to drive instructional decisions and provide specific, timely, growth-oriented feedback rather than simply assigning grades.

items: Formative assessment guides ongoing instruction; summative measures end-of-unit mastery.
Diagnostic assessment reveals prior knowledge and needs before teaching begins.
Quality assessments are valid, reliable, aligned to objectives, and bias-free.
Use varied methods: observations, performance tasks, portfolios, rubrics, and tests.
Analyze data to reteach, group, and differentiate instruction.
Provide specific, timely, actionable feedback focused on growth, not just grades.

topics.title: Piaget vs. Vygotsky: Two Views of Learning

blocks.text: Jean Piaget and Lev Vygotsky both transformed how educators understand cognitive development, yet they emphasized different engines of growth. Piaget viewed development as an internal, largely universal process unfolding through four stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational. For Piaget, children construct knowledge by acting on their environment, using assimilation and accommodation to reach equilibrium. Learning generally follows readiness, so a child must reach a stage before certain reasoning becomes possible. Vygotsky, by contrast, placed culture, language, and social interaction at the center. He argued that learning leads development and that children grow through guided participation with more knowledgeable others. His Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) describes the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with support, while scaffolding provides temporary, fading assistance. In the classroom, Piaget supports discovery learning, hands-on exploration, and developmentally appropriate, concrete materials. Vygotsky supports collaborative grouping, think-alouds, modeling, and dialogue-rich instruction. A skilled teacher blends both: providing exploratory, age-appropriate tasks while also using scaffolds, peer collaboration, and targeted support pitched within each student's ZPD to move learning forward intentionally.

items: Piaget: development drives learning through four universal stages and equilibration (assimilation/accommodation).
Vygotsky: learning drives development through social interaction, language, and culture.
ZPD = the space between independent performance and supported performance; teach here.
Scaffolding offers temporary support that is gradually removed as competence grows.
Piaget supports discovery learning and developmentally appropriate concrete tasks.
Vygotsky supports collaboration, modeling, think-alouds, and guided dialogue.

blocks.text: Bloom's Taxonomy classifies cognitive demand from lower-order to higher-order thinking, giving teachers a shared language for designing questions, tasks, and assessments. The revised version uses six action-verb levels: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. Lower levels build foundational knowledge, while higher levels demand transfer, judgment, and originality. The taxonomy is not strictly hierarchical in classrooms, students can analyze or create while still solidifying facts, but it helps teachers avoid spending all instructional time at recall. In practice, teachers align verbs to objectives: 'list' and 'define' signal Remember, while 'compare,' 'justify,' and 'design' push thinking upward. Effective planning intentionally distributes cognitive demand so all learners access content and are stretched. Bloom's also guides differentiation, advanced learners may begin at Evaluate or Create, while others scaffold up from Understand. On assessments, the taxonomy ensures items measure genuine reasoning rather than memorization alone. For the PPR exam, recognize that strong instruction targets a range of levels, that higher-order questions promote deeper engagement, and that the goal is moving students beyond recall toward analysis, evaluation, and creation across the curriculum.

items: Six revised levels: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create.
Lower levels build foundations; higher levels demand transfer and judgment.
Action verbs in objectives signal the intended cognitive level.
Balanced instruction targets multiple levels, not just recall.
Higher-order questioning promotes deeper engagement and critical thinking.
Use the taxonomy to differentiate entry points and challenge.

blocks.text: Differentiation is the proactive, planned practice of adjusting instruction so every learner can access rigorous content and demonstrate growth. Carol Ann Tomlinson frames differentiation across four classroom elements: content (what students learn), process (how they make sense of it), product (how they show mastery), and learning environment (the physical and emotional climate). Teachers differentiate based on students' readiness, interests, and learning profiles. Importantly, differentiation maintains high expectations for all, it changes the route, not the destination. Strategies include tiered assignments, flexible grouping, choice boards, learning centers, varied texts at multiple reading levels, and graphic organizers. Pre-assessment data drives decisions so support targets actual needs rather than assumptions. Differentiation overlaps with, but differs from, accommodations and modifications: accommodations change how a student accesses learning, modifications change what is expected, and differentiation is good first-tier teaching for everyone. For English learners, this means scaffolds like visuals, sentence stems, and native-language supports; for gifted learners, it means depth, complexity, and acceleration. The PPR exam emphasizes that differentiation is responsive and ongoing, grounded in knowing students well, and aimed at equitable access to challenging curriculum for the full range of learners.

items: Differentiate four elements: content, process, product, and environment.
Base decisions on readiness, interest, and learning profile.
Maintain high expectations, change the path, not the rigor.
Use tiered tasks, flexible grouping, choice, and varied texts.
Pre-assessment data should drive differentiation choices.
Distinguish differentiation from accommodations and modifications.

blocks.text: Assessment serves two complementary purposes, and skilled teachers use both strategically. Formative assessment is assessment FOR learning: ongoing, low-stakes checks that occur during instruction to reveal what students understand and to guide next steps. Examples include exit tickets, thumbs-up/down, whiteboard responses, observation, questioning, and quick quizzes. Its defining feature is feedback that loops back into teaching and learning while there is still time to adjust. Summative assessment is assessment OF learning: it evaluates mastery at the end of a unit or course, often for grades or accountability, such as unit tests, final projects, and state exams like STAAR. A useful metaphor: formative assessment is the cook tasting the soup, summative is the customer tasting it. Both must be valid (measuring what was taught), reliable (consistent), and aligned to objectives. Teachers should weight learning toward frequent formative cycles, because data used in the moment improves outcomes more than data collected only at the end. Diagnostic assessment, given before instruction, identifies prior knowledge and gaps. For the PPR exam, know that formative data drives instructional adjustment and differentiation, while summative data documents achievement, and that effective teachers integrate both purposefully.

items: Formative = assessment FOR learning, ongoing and low-stakes, guides instruction.
Summative = assessment OF learning, evaluates mastery, often graded.
Diagnostic assessment precedes instruction to reveal prior knowledge.
Formative feedback must loop back while there is time to adjust.
Examples: exit tickets and observation (formative); unit tests and STAAR (summative).
All assessments should be valid, reliable, and aligned to objectives.

blocks.text: Strong lessons begin with clarity about what students will know and be able to do. Measurable objectives state observable outcomes using precise action verbs (identify, compare, construct) rather than vague terms like 'understand' or 'know.' A classic frame is ABCD: Audience (the student), Behavior (the observable action), Condition (the circumstances), and Degree (the criterion for success). Objectives must align to standards, in Texas, the TEKS, and to assessments. Backward design, developed by Wiggins and McTighe, reverses traditional planning into three stages: first identify desired results (the goals and enduring understandings), then determine acceptable evidence (how mastery will be demonstrated), and only then plan learning experiences and instruction. This prevents 'activity-oriented' teaching where engaging tasks lack a clear purpose. Backward design ensures coherence among objectives, assessments, and activities, sometimes called alignment. It also pushes teachers to define success criteria before choosing activities, so instruction targets the right destination. For the PPR exam, recognize that measurable objectives drive assessment and instructional choices, that vague objectives cannot be assessed, and that beginning with the end in mind produces tightly aligned, purposeful lessons that move all students toward mastery of required standards.

items: Measurable objectives use observable action verbs, not 'understand' or 'know.'
ABCD frame: Audience, Behavior, Condition, Degree (criterion).
Objectives must align to standards (TEKS) and to assessments.
Backward design: results first, then evidence, then learning activities.
Define how mastery is demonstrated before planning instruction.
Alignment among objectives, assessment, and activities ensures coherence.
Avoid activity-driven teaching that lacks a clear learning target.

blocks.text: Effective instruction respects how the brain takes in, holds, and stores information. The information-processing model traces learning from sensory memory, where stimuli linger for fractions of a second, into working memory, the conscious workspace that can juggle only a handful of items at once, and finally into long-term memory, the durable network where knowledge is encoded as schemas. Working memory's narrow capacity is the central constraint teachers must honor. Cognitive load theory distinguishes intrinsic load (the inherent difficulty of content), extraneous load (clutter from poor design), and germane load (the productive effort of building schemas). Skilled teachers slash extraneous load through clear examples, worked problems, and uncluttered slides while sequencing content so intrinsic load stays manageable. Attention acts as the gateway: nothing enters working memory unnoticed, so novelty, relevance, and purposeful cues matter. Encoding deepens when learners connect new material to prior knowledge, elaborate, and organize ideas meaningfully rather than rehearse passively. Retrieval practice, spacing, and interleaving strengthen durable recall far more than rereading. As learners gain expertise, related elements chunk into automatic units, freeing working memory for higher-order thinking. The EC-12 teacher applies these principles by activating prior knowledge, chunking, modeling, and building in frequent retrieval so that fragile new learning becomes lasting, transferable understanding.

items: Sensory, working, and long-term memory form a pipeline; working memory's limited capacity (a few items) is the key bottleneck.
Reduce extraneous cognitive load with clean design and worked examples; manage intrinsic load through sequencing and scaffolding.
Attention is the gateway to learning—use relevance, novelty, and explicit cues to direct it.
Meaningful encoding (connecting to prior knowledge, elaboration, organization) outperforms rote rehearsal.
Retrieval practice, spaced review, and interleaving build durable, transferable memory better than rereading.
Chunking and automaticity free working-memory resources for higher-order reasoning.
Activate prior knowledge before new content so learners have a schema to attach it to.

blocks.text: Culturally responsive teaching positions students' cultural backgrounds, languages, and lived experiences as assets that fuel learning rather than obstacles to overcome. It rests on the conviction that every learner brings funds of knowledge—skills, traditions, and ways of knowing accumulated at home and in community—that teachers can leverage to make content relevant and accessible. The approach begins with the teacher's own critical self-reflection on biases, assumptions, and the dominant cultural lens embedded in curriculum and assessment. From there, the teacher builds authentic relationships, communicates high expectations for all, and designs instruction that connects new concepts to students' realities through varied texts, examples, and perspectives. Culturally responsive classrooms validate home languages and dialects while still developing academic proficiency, and they incorporate diverse voices not as token add-ons but as central content. Equity, distinct from equality, means allocating support based on need so each student can reach rigorous goals. Responsive teachers also cultivate sociopolitical awareness, helping students examine fairness and use academic skills to address real issues. Crucially, this is not lowering standards; it is widening pathways to meet them. By honoring identity, the teacher increases engagement, belonging, and achievement—core aims reflected throughout the PPR framework for serving Texas's diverse EC-12 population with dignity and rigor.

items: Treat students' cultures, languages, and funds of knowledge as assets to build on, not deficits to fix.
Begin with self-reflection on personal biases and the cultural assumptions embedded in curriculum and assessment.
Pair warm relationships and a sense of belonging with consistently high expectations for every learner.
Equity means distributing support by need; equality means identical treatment—they are not the same.
Validate home languages and dialects while developing academic English and rigorous content mastery.
Integrate diverse perspectives as central content, avoiding tokenism or surface-level 'heroes and holidays.'
Responsiveness raises engagement and achievement; it never means reducing rigor or expectations.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Writing Quality Assessment Items

blocks.text: Sound assessment items measure exactly what the learning objective intends—no more, no less. The process starts with alignment: each item should map to a specific objective and an appropriate cognitive level, so a recall objective is checked with recall items and an analysis objective demands analysis. Validity asks whether the item measures the intended construct, while reliability asks whether it yields consistent results; both can be undermined by careless writing. For selected-response items, stems should pose a clear, complete problem, distractors must be plausible and based on common misconceptions, and answer choices should be parallel in length and grammar to avoid unintended clues. Teachers must root out cueing, double negatives, 'all of the above' traps, and culturally loaded or ambiguous wording that turns a content question into a reading or background-knowledge test. Constructed-response and performance tasks tap higher-order thinking but require clear prompts and well-defined rubrics with descriptive criteria to ensure fair, consistent scoring. A useful test blueprint balances item types and cognitive levels across the content sampled. Formative items inform instruction; summative items document mastery—item design should fit the purpose. Strong items minimize bias, accommodate diverse learners, and produce data the teacher can actually use to adjust teaching and support student growth.

items: Align every item to a specific objective and matching cognitive level (recall vs. application vs. analysis).
Validity = measures the intended construct; reliability = yields consistent results—write to protect both.
Craft clear stems and plausible distractors built from real student misconceptions.
Eliminate flaws: cueing, grammatical clues, double negatives, ambiguity, and culturally biased wording.
Use rubrics with descriptive criteria for constructed-response and performance tasks to ensure fair scoring.
Build a blueprint that balances item types and cognitive levels across the content tested.
Match item design to purpose—formative items guide instruction, summative items certify mastery.

blocks.text: Scaffolding is the temporary, adjustable support a teacher provides so a learner can accomplish a task just beyond independent reach, then withdraws as competence grows. It lives inside Vygotsky's zone of proximal development: the space between what a student can do alone and what they can do with guidance. The gradual release of responsibility model operationalizes scaffolding through four phases often summarized as 'I do, we do, you do together, you do alone.' First the teacher models thinking aloud, making invisible cognition visible. Next, shared practice invites students to participate while the teacher leads. Then collaborative practice shifts ownership to peers working interdependently. Finally, independent practice confirms transfer. Effective scaffolds are contingent (matched to the learner's current need), faded over time, and transferred so the student internalizes the strategy. Examples include sentence stems, worked examples, graphic organizers, think-alouds, cue cards, and chunked tasks. The art lies in fading: scaffolds left in place too long create dependence, while removing them too soon causes frustration and failure. On the PPR exam, watch for scenarios asking which support best matches a struggling learner, or how a teacher should adjust support over a unit. The correct answer usually preserves rigor while making the cognitive load manageable and explicitly plans for release toward autonomy and self-regulation.

items: Scaffolding works within the zone of proximal development; aim just beyond independent skill, not far above it.
Gradual release moves through I do (model), we do (guided), you do together (collaborative), you do alone (independent).
Quality scaffolds are contingent, faded, and transferred so students eventually self-direct.
Common scaffolds: think-alouds, worked examples, sentence stems, graphic organizers, chunking, and cue cards.
Fading is essential; permanent scaffolds breed dependence while premature removal causes failure.
Scaffolding lowers cognitive load without lowering rigor or learning expectations.
On exam items, choose responses that adjust support to the learner and plan for eventual independence.

blocks.text: Validity and reliability are the two pillars of trustworthy assessment, and they are not interchangeable. Reliability concerns consistency: would a student earn roughly the same score if tested again, scored by another teacher, or assessed on a parallel form? Validity concerns accuracy: does the assessment actually measure the intended learning target? A test can be reliable yet invalid, like a precise scale that consistently reads five pounds heavy. The reverse, however, is impossible: an unreliable assessment cannot be valid because inconsistent results cannot accurately measure anything. Teachers boost reliability with clear rubrics, multiple items per objective, standardized administration, and inter-rater calibration. They strengthen validity by aligning items directly to objectives (content validity), ensuring questions tap the intended cognitive level, and removing construct-irrelevant barriers such as confusing wording or unnecessary reading load on a math test. Bias and lack of accessibility threaten validity because they introduce factors unrelated to the construct. On the PPR, expect scenarios where a teacher gets puzzling results and must diagnose the cause: a reading-heavy science test penalizes English learners (validity), or two graders score essays differently (reliability). The strongest answers tie the assessment back to its purpose and the learning objective, and favor multiple measures over a single high-stakes snapshot when making decisions about students.

items: Reliability equals consistency across time, raters, and forms; validity equals measuring what you intend to measure.
An assessment can be reliable but invalid; it can never be valid without being reliable.
Content validity means items align tightly to stated objectives and the right cognitive level.
Improve reliability with clear rubrics, multiple items, standardized conditions, and rater calibration.

Reduce bias and increase accessibility so results reflect the construct, not unrelated barriers.
Prefer multiple measures over one high-stakes test when making decisions about students.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Backward Design (Understanding by Design)

blocks.text: Backward design, popularized by Wiggins and McTighe in Understanding by Design, reverses the intuitive lesson-planning order. Instead of starting with activities or a favorite textbook chapter, teachers begin with the end in mind and work backward through three stages. Stage one identifies desired results: what enduring understandings, essential questions, and specific knowledge and skills should endure long after the unit ends? Teachers prioritize the 'big ideas' worth transferring over a sprawl of disconnected facts. Stage two determines acceptable evidence: how will students demonstrate they truly understand, not just recall? This is where assessments and performance tasks are designed before instruction, ensuring the test measures the targeted goals rather than being bolted on afterward. Stage three plans learning experiences and instruction: only now does the teacher select activities, resources, and sequencing, choosing them deliberately because they build toward the established goals and assessments. The payoff is tight alignment among objectives, assessment, and instruction, which prevents the common trap of 'activity-oriented' or 'coverage-oriented' teaching where engaging tasks lack a clear learning purpose. On the PPR, backward design surfaces in items about planning coherent units, aligning assessment to objectives, and focusing on transferable understanding. The best answers start from clearly defined learning goals and let those goals drive every assessment and activity decision that follows.

items: Backward design plans in three stages: desired results, acceptable evidence, then learning experiences.
Begin with enduring understandings and essential questions, not activities or textbook chapters.
Design assessments before instruction so they measure the targeted goals, not afterthoughts.

The method guarantees alignment among objectives, assessment, and instruction.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Multiple Intelligences vs. Learning Styles

blocks.text: Beginning teachers often blur two distinct ideas. Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences proposes that human ability spans several relatively independent capacities, such as linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalist. Gardner intended these as profiles of strength, not as fixed teaching channels. The popular learning styles claim, by contrast, asserts that each learner has a single preferred sensory mode, visual, auditory, or kinesthetic, and that matching instruction to that mode raises achievement. Decades of controlled research have failed to confirm this matching hypothesis, so a defensible Texas teacher does not sort students into one channel and limit them to it. The PPR-aligned takeaway is nuanced. Recognize that learners differ, value those differences, and design lessons that engage content through multiple representations because rich material is best learned in multiple modalities, not because each child needs a private style. Use intelligence profiles to broaden entry points and to honor varied strengths, while always anchoring choices to the lesson objective and the nature of the content itself. Avoid labeling students or excusing low expectations. The strongest answer on the exam treats variety as a tool for access and engagement for all students, rejects rigid style matching, and keeps rigorous, grade-level learning goals constant for every learner in the room.

items: Gardner's multiple intelligences describe profiles of strength, not teaching channels to which students must be matched.
The learning-styles matching hypothesis (V-A-K) lacks research support; do not lock students into one sensory mode.
Use multiple representations because content is best learned in multiple modalities, not to match a fixed 'style.'
Always tie instructional variety to the lesson objective and the nature of the content.
Never use intelligences or styles to label students or to lower expectations for any learner.

blocks.text: Effective planning begins with knowing what students already understand. Diagnostic and pre-assessment gather evidence before instruction so teachers can target a unit to real needs rather than assumptions. A pre-assessment measures prior knowledge and skill against upcoming objectives, while a diagnostic assessment probes more deeply to locate specific gaps, misconceptions, or readiness levels. Neither is graded for a mark; their purpose is information, not evaluation. Useful forms include short ungraded quizzes, K-W-L charts, concept maps, entry tickets, structured interviews, running records in reading, and analysis of prior work samples. The data should drive concrete decisions: which prerequisite skills need reteaching, which students are ready for extension, how to form flexible groups, and where to set the lesson's starting point. On the PPR exam, the key distinction is timing and intent. Diagnostic and pre-assessment occur before or at the very start of a unit to inform planning; formative assessment occurs during learning to adjust instruction; summative assessment occurs after to judge mastery. A strong teacher closes the loop by actually changing plans based on what the pre-assessment reveals, communicates purpose so students do not fear the ungraded task, and revisits the diagnostic picture as the unit unfolds. The wrong answer assumes all learners begin at the same place; the right answer lets evidence shape responsive, differentiated planning.

items: Pre-assessment measures prior knowledge against upcoming objectives; diagnostic assessment locates specific gaps and misconceptions.
Both occur before or at the start of instruction and are ungraded; their purpose is information, not evaluation.
Tools include K-W-L charts, concept maps, entry tickets, short quizzes, interviews, running records, and work samples.
Data should drive flexible grouping, reteaching of prerequisites, extension for ready students, and the lesson's entry point.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Vertical Alignment & the TEKS

blocks.text: The Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills, or TEKS, are the state-adopted standards that define what students must learn in each subject and grade. Vertical alignment refers to how those standards build coherently from one grade to the next, so that a skill introduced in an early grade is deepened and extended later rather than repeated or skipped. Understanding vertical alignment lets a teacher see where a current objective came from and where it is heading, which informs both reteaching of prerequisite knowledge and appropriate stretching toward the next grade's demands. Horizontal alignment, by contrast, concerns coherence across a single grade or course among teachers, units, and assessments within the same year. A well-aligned teacher unpacks each TEKS into its verbs and concepts, identifies the cognitive demand, and ensures instruction and assessment actually target that standard. On the PPR exam, expect scenarios where you must select objectives that match the TEKS, plan backward from the standard, or recognize that a colleague should consult prior- and next-grade expectations when students struggle or excel. The defensible choice keeps the standard, not the textbook or a favorite activity, as the anchor for planning. Strong teachers collaborate vertically across grade levels, use the TEKS to set rigorous and measurable objectives, and design assessments that provide evidence specifically of the targeted standard.

items: TEKS are the Texas state standards defining required knowledge and skills by subject and grade.
Vertical alignment is coherence across grades; horizontal alignment is coherence within a single grade or course.
Unpack each TEKS into verbs and concepts to identify its cognitive demand before planning.
