blocks.text: Cognitive Load Theory explains how the limited capacity of working memory shapes whether new information ever reaches long-term memory. Because learners can hold only a few elements at once, instruction that overwhelms working memory stalls learning, while instruction that manages it accelerates it. Educators distinguish three load types. Intrinsic load reflects the inherent difficulty of the material and the number of interacting elements a student must process simultaneously. Extraneous load is the unnecessary mental effort imposed by confusing layouts, irrelevant details, or poorly sequenced tasks; teachers can and should reduce it. Germane load is the productive effort devoted to building durable mental schemas. The teacher's task is to lower extraneous load, calibrate intrinsic load to the learner's prior knowledge, and channel freed capacity toward germane processing. Practical moves include presenting worked examples before independent practice, pairing visuals with spoken rather than written words to avoid splitting attention, chunking content, and gradually removing scaffolds as expertise grows. Importantly, what helps novices can hinder experts, a phenomenon called the expertise reversal effect, so supports must fade over time. For the TExES, candidates connect Cognitive Load Theory to lesson sequencing, pacing, scaffolding, and differentiation decisions that respect how memory actually works.

items: Working memory is severely limited; long-term memory is vast, so instruction must move information into schemas without overloading the bottleneck.
Distinguish intrinsic (inherent difficulty), extraneous (avoidable, instruction-caused), and germane (productive schema-building) load.
Reduce extraneous load by eliminating clutter, avoiding split-attention, and sequencing logically; this frees capacity for learning.
Use worked examples and partially completed problems before full independent practice, especially for novices.
Apply the expertise reversal effect: fade scaffolds as students gain proficiency because supports that help beginners slow experts.
Calibrate intrinsic load to prior knowledge through chunking, pre-teaching vocabulary, and activating relevant background.
Tie the theory to concrete planning choices: pacing, scaffolding, modality pairing, and differentiation.

blocks.text: A rubric is a scoring tool that makes the expectations for quality work explicit by laying out criteria and describing performance across levels. Well-built rubrics improve consistency among scorers, clarify targets for students, and turn grading into feedback rather than a mysterious verdict. Teachers choose among formats based on purpose. Analytic rubrics score each criterion separately, yielding detailed diagnostic information useful for instruction and revision. Holistic rubrics assign a single overall judgment, which is faster for high-volume or summative scoring but less informative. Single-point rubrics describe only proficiency, leaving open space to note specific strengths and growth areas, which keeps feedback personalized. Effective design begins with the learning objective: criteria must measure what truly matters, not merely what is easy to count, such as page length. Performance-level descriptors should use concrete, observable language and describe meaningful qualitative differences rather than vague comparatives like 'somewhat' or 'mostly.' Sharing rubrics before an assignment, co-constructing them with students, and using exemplars to anchor each level all deepen understanding of quality. To strengthen reliability, teachers calibrate by scoring sample work together. On the TExES, candidates recognize rubrics as instruments of fairness, transparency, formative feedback, and alignment between objectives, instruction, and assessment.

items: Rubrics increase scoring consistency, communicate expectations clearly, and convert grading into actionable feedback.
Choose analytic rubrics for diagnostic detail, holistic for efficient overall judgments, and single-point to highlight individualized growth.
Derive criteria directly from learning objectives so the rubric measures what matters, not just what is easy to count.
Write descriptors in concrete, observable language with meaningful distinctions between levels, avoiding vague qualifiers.
Share rubrics in advance, co-construct with students, and use exemplars to anchor each performance level.
Calibrate with colleagues on sample work to strengthen inter-rater reliability and fairness.
Ensure tight alignment among objectives, instruction, and the rubric to support valid assessment.

sections.title: Creating a Positive, Productive Classroom Environment
sections.summary: 13 lessons for Domain 2 (13% of the exam).

topics.title: Creating a Positive, Equitable Classroom Climate

blocks.text: A productive classroom rests on a climate that is safe, respectful, supportive, and equitable. Teachers intentionally build relationships, communicate care, and establish norms that foster mutual respect and a sense of belonging for every student. A positive climate encourages risk-taking, persistence, and collaboration while reducing anxiety and behavioral problems. Teachers set high expectations communicated equitably to all learners and avoid favoritism or bias. They organize the physical and emotional environment to maximize engagement, accessibility, and student comfort. Equity means responsiveness to each student's needs so all can succeed, not identical treatment. Teachers cultivate rapport, fairness, and consistency, model respect, and address conflict constructively. They create structures—classroom community-building, clear routines, and shared values—that promote responsibility and self-discipline. Cultural sensitivity ensures all students feel valued. A strong climate also supports social and emotional development, helping students regulate emotions and build positive peer relationships. The exam stresses that learning thrives when students feel known, respected, safe, and capable, and that the teacher is responsible for deliberately establishing these conditions.

items: Build a safe, respectful, supportive climate where all students feel they belong.
Strong teacher-student relationships increase engagement and reduce misbehavior.
Set and communicate high expectations equitably to every learner.
Equity means responsiveness to individual needs, not identical treatment.
Organize the physical and emotional environment to maximize engagement and access.
Model respect, fairness, and consistency; address conflict constructively.
Support social-emotional development and a sense of community.

blocks.text: Effective classroom management creates the conditions for learning by maximizing time on task and minimizing disruption through proactive structures rather than reactive discipline. Teachers establish clear rules, routines, and procedures early, teach them explicitly, and reinforce them consistently. Smooth transitions, efficient use of materials, and well-planned pacing reduce off-task behavior. Engagement is the strongest management tool: when lessons are relevant, active, and appropriately challenging, students stay focused. Teachers use varied strategies, active participation, and meaningful tasks to sustain attention and motivation. They monitor the room continually (with-it-ness), anticipate problems, and respond to minor issues quickly and calmly before they escalate. Effective managers apply logical, consistent, and fair consequences, emphasize positive reinforcement, and teach self-management and responsibility. Behavior support is respectful and aims to keep students learning, not merely to punish. The exam emphasizes prevention—clear expectations, engaging instruction, strong relationships, and consistent routines—over punitive control, and expects teachers to balance structure with flexibility to keep all students productively engaged.

items: Establish, teach, and consistently reinforce rules, routines, and procedures early.
Maximize time on task with smooth transitions and efficient pacing.
Engaging, relevant, appropriately challenging instruction prevents misbehavior.
Use with-it-ness: monitor continually and address minor issues before they escalate.
Apply consequences that are logical, consistent, and fair; emphasize positive reinforcement.
Teach self-management and responsibility, not just compliance.
Favor proactive prevention over reactive, punitive control.

blocks.text: Effective classroom management rests on prevention, relationships, and consistency rather than reaction. Several influential models inform Texas teachers' practice. The Kounin model emphasizes 'withitness' (awareness of everything happening), overlapping (handling multiple events at once), smooth transitions, and group focus, the proactive teacher prevents problems before they spread. Canter's Assertive Discipline stresses clear expectations, firm but caring follow-through, and consistent consequences communicated calmly. Glasser's Choice Theory and reality therapy view behavior as a choice driven by needs, encouraging students to take responsibility and the teacher to build a needs-satisfying environment. Restorative practices shift focus from punishment to repairing harm, restoring relationships, and reintegrating students into the community through dialogue and accountability. Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) provides a tiered, schoolwide framework that teaches and reinforces expected behaviors. Across models, common threads emerge: establish clear rules, build positive relationships, teach expectations explicitly, respond consistently and fairly, and protect instructional time. The PPR exam favors proactive, relationship-centered, and least-intrusive approaches, addressing minor issues privately, using logical consequences, and preserving student dignity, over punitive or escalating reactions. The goal is self-regulation and a safe, respectful learning community.

items: Kounin: withitness, overlapping, smooth transitions, and group focus prevent disruption.
Canter's Assertive Discipline: clear expectations and consistent, calm follow-through.
Glasser: behavior is a choice driven by needs; build responsibility.
Restorative practices repair harm and restore relationships over punishment.
PBIS: tiered, schoolwide teaching and reinforcement of expected behaviors.
Prevention and relationships matter more than reaction.
Favor least-intrusive, dignity-preserving, consistent responses.

blocks.text: Motivation explains why students engage, persist, and invest effort, and teachers shape it daily. Intrinsic motivation comes from within: curiosity, interest, mastery, and the satisfaction of learning itself. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards or pressures: grades, stickers, praise, or avoiding consequences. Both have a place, but research warns that over-reliance on extrinsic rewards can erode intrinsic interest (the overjustification effect). Self-Determination Theory (Deci and Ryan) identifies three innate psychological needs that fuel intrinsic motivation: autonomy (meaningful choice and ownership), competence (feeling capable through appropriate challenge and feedback), and relatedness (belonging and positive connection). When teachers meet these needs, students engage more deeply and persist longer. Related ideas include attribution theory (students attribute success to effort, ability, luck, or task difficulty, effort attributions support a growth mindset), Dweck's growth versus fixed mindset, and the importance of relevance and goal-setting. Maslow's hierarchy reminds teachers that basic and safety needs must be met before higher learning. For the PPR exam, prioritize strategies that build intrinsic motivation, offering choice, connecting learning to students' lives, ensuring achievable challenge, praising effort and strategy, and fostering belonging, while using extrinsic rewards sparingly and purposefully.

items: Intrinsic motivation comes from interest and mastery; extrinsic from outside rewards.
Overusing extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic interest (overjustification).
Self-Determination Theory: autonomy, competence, and relatedness drive engagement.
Attribution to effort and a growth mindset support persistence.
Relevance and meaningful choice increase ownership and motivation.
Maslow: basic needs must be met before higher-level learning.
Praise effort and strategy; use extrinsic rewards sparingly.

blocks.text: Procedures and routines are the invisible architecture of a smoothly running classroom, and they are central to the work of Harry Wong and others. A procedure is the way something is done (how to turn in work, line up, ask for help); a routine is a procedure that has become automatic through practice. Well-established routines reduce disruptions, maximize instructional time, lower student anxiety by making expectations predictable, and free the teacher to focus on instruction rather than control. The most effective teachers invest heavily in teaching procedures during the first weeks of school, treating them like academic content. The process is explicit: teach the procedure (explain and model), rehearse it (practice with feedback), and reinforce it (reteach and recognize until it becomes routine). Procedures should be specific, positively stated, and few enough to remember. Key areas include entering and exiting, transitions, materials, group work, restroom and emergencies, and signals for attention. Consistency across days and adults is essential, inconsistency breeds confusion and testing. For the PPR exam, recognize that strong management is proactive and rooted in taught routines, that the opening weeks are critical, and that predictable structures support all learners, especially those who thrive on clear expectations.

items: Procedures define how tasks are done; routines are procedures made automatic.
Strong routines maximize instructional time and reduce disruptions.
Teach procedures explicitly: explain, model, rehearse, and reinforce.
Invest heavily in routines during the first weeks of school.
Keep procedures specific, positively stated, and few in number.
Consistency across days and adults prevents confusion and testing.
Predictable structures lower anxiety and support all learners.

blocks.text: The strongest classroom management is invisible because it prevents problems before they start. Proactive management means designing the environment, routines, and instruction so that misbehavior has little room to grow. Clear expectations taught and practiced like academic content, efficient transitions, engaging pacing, and consistent procedures reduce the idle time and confusion that breed off-task behavior. Withitness—the teacher's awareness of everything happening across the room—lets small issues be addressed quietly before they escalate, while proximity, nonverbal cues, and brief redirections handle minor disruptions without stopping the lesson. When a student does begin to escalate, de-escalation skills protect dignity and safety. The teacher stays calm, lowers voice and tension, allows space and processing time, and avoids power struggles that force a student to save face by digging in. Listening to the underlying need, offering limited choices, and validating feelings while holding the boundary often defuse conflict faster than confrontation. Behavior is communication; identifying its function guides a more effective response. Logical consequences delivered privately and consistently preserve the relationship and teach responsibility. Teachers also recognize escalation cycles and trauma-related triggers, responding with regulation rather than reaction. The aim is a safe, predictable, respectful climate where students learn to self-manage and instructional time is protected.

items: Prevention beats reaction: clear routines, engaging pacing, and taught expectations stop most problems before they start.
Use 'withitness,' proximity, and nonverbal cues to address minor issues without interrupting instruction.
During escalation, stay calm, lower your voice, allow space, and avoid public power struggles.
Treat behavior as communication—identify its function to choose the right response.
Offer limited choices and validate feelings while still holding firm, consistent boundaries.
Deliver logical consequences privately and consistently to preserve dignity and the relationship.
Recognize escalation cycles and trauma triggers; respond with regulation, not reaction.

blocks.text: A strong classroom community is the foundation on which both behavior and learning rest. When students feel safe, known, and valued, they take intellectual risks, persist through difficulty, and treat one another with respect. Community building begins on day one and continues all year through intentional relationship work: learning names and stories, greeting students individually, and showing genuine interest in their lives. Co-creating norms with students rather than imposing rules fosters ownership and shared accountability. A positive climate balances warmth with structure—high expectations communicated through belief in every student's capacity, paired with the consistency that makes the room feel predictable and fair. Teachers nurture peer relationships through collaborative structures, class meetings, and restorative practices that repair harm and rebuild trust instead of merely punishing. Social-emotional learning—self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making—is woven into daily interactions, giving students the tools to navigate conflict and emotion. Belonging is especially vital for students who have felt marginalized; representation, inclusion, and affirmation signal that everyone has a place. A teacher who models respect, fairness, and emotional regulation sets the tone the class mirrors. The payoff is a setting where intrinsic motivation, cooperation, and engagement flourish, and where managing behavior becomes a matter of maintaining relationships rather than enforcing compliance.

items: Belonging and psychological safety enable risk-taking, persistence, and engagement.
Invest early and continuously in relationships—know each student's name, story, and strengths.
Co-create norms with students to build ownership and shared accountability.
Balance warmth with structure: high expectations plus predictable, fair consistency.
Use restorative practices to repair harm and rebuild trust rather than just punish.
Integrate SEL competencies into daily routines so students can manage emotion and conflict.
Model the respect, fairness, and regulation you expect the class to mirror.

blocks.text: Jacob Kounin's research reshaped classroom management by showing that the most effective teachers prevent misbehavior through skilled lesson management rather than reacting after problems erupt. His signature concept is 'withitness': the teacher's demonstrated awareness of everything happening in the room, communicated so convincingly that students believe the teacher has eyes in the back of the head. Withit teachers catch the right student at the right moment, before a minor disruption spreads. Closely related is 'overlapping,' the ability to attend to two events at once, such as helping a small group while monitoring the rest of the class with a glance or a quiet cue. Kounin also identified 'momentum' and 'smoothness,' the steady pacing and seamless transitions that keep lessons flowing; their enemies are 'jerkiness' and 'slowdowns' caused by overdwelling or fragmenting tasks. The 'ripple effect' describes how correcting one student influences the behavior of onlookers, for better or worse. 'Group alerting' and 'accountability' keep all learners attentive by signaling that anyone may be called on and their work will be checked. On the PPR, these principles appear in scenarios where the strongest response is proactive and minimally disruptive: a brief glance, proximity, or a redirect that preserves instructional momentum rather than stopping the lesson to confront a student.

items: Withitness is communicated awareness of all classroom activity, enabling early, accurate intervention.
Overlapping is managing two or more events simultaneously without losing control of either.
Momentum and smoothness keep pacing brisk and transitions seamless; avoid jerkiness and slowdowns.
The ripple effect means correcting one student influences the watching group.
Group alerting and accountability keep every student engaged and responsible for the work.
Effective management is preventive and proactive, not merely reactive to misbehavior.
Favor low-intervention moves (proximity, glance, brief redirect) that preserve instructional flow.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Responding to Challenging Behavior

blocks.text: Responding to challenging behavior begins with a mindset shift: behavior is communication, and every disruptive act serves a function, usually to gain something (attention, a desired item, control) or to escape something (a hard task, an uncomfortable setting). Effective teachers respond along a continuum of least-to-most intrusive interventions, escalating only as needed. The gentlest tools are nonverbal: planned ignoring of attention-seeking behavior, proximity, eye contact, and a private signal. Next come low-key verbal moves: a quiet redirect, restating the expectation, or offering a structured choice that returns control to the student while keeping the boundary firm. Only when these fail does the teacher move to logical consequences, a private conference, or a documented referral. Throughout, the teacher stays calm, avoids power struggles, separates the behavior from the child's worth, and preserves the student's dignity to prevent escalation. For persistent patterns, schools use a functional behavior assessment to identify the behavior's purpose, then build a behavior intervention plan that teaches and reinforces a replacement behavior meeting the same need more appropriately. Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports frames this within a tiered, prevention-first system. On the PPR, the best answers diagnose why the behavior occurs, choose the least intrusive effective response, teach an appropriate alternative, and reinforce positive behavior rather than relying on punishment alone.

items: Behavior is communication; most misbehavior functions to obtain something or escape something.
Intervene along a continuum from least to most intrusive, escalating only when necessary.
Use nonverbal tools first: planned ignoring, proximity, signals, then quiet verbal redirects.
Offer structured choices to return control while holding the boundary firm.
Stay calm, avoid power struggles, and preserve the student's dignity to prevent escalation.
For persistent patterns, use a functional behavior assessment to drive a behavior intervention plan.
Teach and reinforce replacement behaviors; prevention and positive supports beat punishment alone.

topics.title: Deep Dive: The First Weeks — Establishing Routines

blocks.text: Classroom climate is largely set in the opening weeks, and the most effective teachers invest that time in explicitly teaching procedures rather than only stating rules. A procedure is the predictable way a recurring task is done, entering the room, turning in work, transitioning, sharpening a pencil, asking for help, while a rule is a broad expectation for behavior. Research on effective beginnings shows that smoothly running classrooms result from routines taught the way academic content is taught: explain the procedure, model it, have students rehearse it, give feedback, and reinforce it until it becomes automatic. Investing early reduces lost instructional time, lowers misbehavior caused by uncertainty, and frees attention for learning. Equally important is building relationships and co-constructing a small set of positive, clearly stated expectations, ideally framed as what to do rather than what not to do, and applied consistently and fairly. On the PPR exam, the strongest answers treat misbehavior in the first weeks as a signal that a procedure needs reteaching, not merely punishment, and they emphasize prevention, structure, and warmth together. Teachers should establish predictable signals, organize the physical space to support movement and access, and maintain consistency so students feel safe and know what success looks like. A well-managed start creates the conditions for engagement, equity, and rigorous learning throughout the year.

items: Teach procedures (predictable ways to do recurring tasks) explicitly; rules are broad behavioral expectations.
Use explain-model-rehearse-feedback-reinforce so routines become automatic, just like academic content.
Early investment in routines reduces lost time, prevents uncertainty-driven misbehavior, and protects instruction.
Co-construct a few positive, clearly stated expectations framed as what to do, applied consistently and fairly.
Treat early misbehavior as a cue to reteach a procedure, not only to punish; pair structure with warmth.
Arrange physical space and signals to support smooth transitions, access, and a safe, predictable climate.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Equity and Access in the Classroom

blocks.text: Equity means ensuring every student receives what they need to reach high standards, which is distinct from equality, giving every student the identical resource regardless of need. An equitable classroom removes barriers so that language background, disability, socioeconomic status, gender, race, or readiness does not predetermine achievement. Practically, this means holding consistently high expectations for all learners while varying support, scaffolds, and pathways. Universal Design for Learning offers a proactive frame: provide multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression so access is built in from the start rather than retrofitted. Teachers advance access by checking that all students participate meaningfully, distributing questions and attention equitably, offering scaffolds such as sentence stems, visuals, and native-language supports for emergent bilingual students, and ensuring materials reflect diverse identities. Equity also requires examining one's own biases, low expectations, and patterns in discipline or call-on rates that may disadvantage particular groups. On the PPR exam, the defensible answer never lowers the learning goal; instead it changes the route, the support, or the representation to help each learner meet rigorous, grade-level objectives. Teachers should also know when to seek services, interpreters, accommodations, or specialists to remove barriers. The strongest practice combines warmth and high expectations, sometimes called warm demanding, and treats access as a precondition for engagement, fairness, and genuine learning for every child.

items: Equity gives each student what they need to reach high standards; equality gives identical resources regardless of need.
Hold consistently high expectations for all while varying scaffolds, supports, and pathways.
Use Universal Design for Learning: multiple means of engagement, representation, and action/expression built in proactively.
Provide targeted supports (sentence stems, visuals, native-language aids) and ensure materials reflect diverse identities.
Examine personal bias and patterns in discipline and questioning that may disadvantage specific groups.
Change the route or support, not the goal; seek accommodations, interpreters, or specialists to remove barriers.

blocks.text: Restorative practices reframe discipline as an opportunity to repair relationships and strengthen community rather than simply to punish. Rooted in the question 'who was harmed and what is needed to make things right,' these approaches contrast with traditional punitive models that ask only what rule was broken and what penalty applies. The framework operates on a continuum. Proactive, community-building moves such as morning circles, clear shared norms, and intentional relationship-building prevent conflict by fostering belonging and trust. Responsive practices, including restorative conversations, affective statements, and harm circles, address incidents when they occur by giving those affected a voice, holding the responsible student accountable, and developing a concrete plan to repair harm. The goal is accountability with dignity: students take responsibility, understand the impact of their actions, and remain connected to the community rather than excluded from it. Research links restorative approaches to reduced exclusionary discipline, fewer repeat incidents, and improvements in school climate, with particular promise for narrowing discipline disparities. Successful implementation requires consistency, staff training, administrative support, and genuine cultural commitment rather than treating circles as a one-time event. For the TExES, candidates connect restorative practices to creating safe, supportive, inclusive learning environments and to managing behavior in ways that keep students engaged and in school.

items: Restorative practices shift the focus from punishment to repairing harm and restoring relationships within the community.
Use a continuum: proactive community-building (circles, norms, relationships) plus responsive repair (restorative conversations, harm circles).
Center key questions: who was harmed, what are their needs, and whose obligation is it to make things right.
Aim for accountability with dignity so students take responsibility while staying connected, not excluded.
Affective statements and active listening help students recognize the impact of their behavior on others.
Evidence links the approach to less exclusionary discipline, fewer repeat incidents, and reduced disparities.
Effective use requires training, consistency, and whole-school commitment, not occasional circles.

blocks.text: Engagement is the degree to which students invest attention, effort, and emotion in learning, and it is a strong lever for achievement, motivation, and on-task behavior. Educators distinguish three intertwined dimensions: behavioral engagement (participation and persistence), emotional engagement (interest, belonging, and positive feelings toward school), and cognitive engagement (the willingness to grapple deeply with challenging ideas). High-impact strategies target all three. Maximizing active response opportunities, through techniques such as cold-calling paired with wait time, whole-class signals, choral response, and structured partner talk, ensures every student thinks rather than a few volunteers carrying the lesson. Total participation techniques like think-pair-share, quick writes, and mini whiteboards make thinking visible and give the teacher real-time formative data. Relevance and autonomy fuel emotional investment: connecting content to students' lives, cultures, and goals, and offering meaningful choice, deepens ownership. Appropriately challenging tasks within reach with support sustain cognitive engagement, while clear routines and brisk pacing minimize lost time and behavioral drift. Crucially, engagement should be tied to genuine learning, not mere busyness or entertainment; activity without intellectual demand produces compliance, not growth. For the TExES, candidates recognize engagement strategies as tools that promote equitable participation, formative checking for understanding, and a productive, motivating classroom climate.

items: Engagement spans behavioral (participation), emotional (interest and belonging), and cognitive (deep thinking) dimensions.
Increase active response opportunities with cold-calling plus wait time, choral response, signals, and structured partner talk.
Use total participation techniques (think-pair-share, quick writes, whiteboards) to make all students' thinking visible.
Boost emotional engagement through relevance to students' lives and cultures and through meaningful choice and autonomy.
Sustain cognitive engagement with appropriately challenging tasks supported by scaffolding.
Maintain clear routines and brisk pacing to minimize off-task time without sacrificing depth.
Distinguish genuine intellectual engagement from mere busyness or entertainment.

sections.title: Implementing Effective, Responsive Instruction and Assessment
sections.summary: 20 lessons for Domain 3 (33% of the exam).

blocks.text: Clear, accurate, and engaging communication is central to teaching. Teachers must convey content precisely using language appropriate to students' developmental levels, while also listening actively and reading nonverbal cues. Skilled teachers explain ideas in multiple ways, use accurate vocabulary, and check for understanding frequently. Questioning is a vital communication tool: effective teachers ask a range of questions—from recall to higher-order—provide adequate wait time, distribute questions equitably, and use responses to gauge and extend learning. Communication also includes giving clear directions, modeling, and using examples, analogies, and visuals to make abstract concepts accessible. Teachers foster productive discourse by encouraging student-to-student dialogue, respectful debate, and elaborated responses. Nonverbal communication—tone, gestures, proximity, eye contact—shapes the classroom message and supports management. Teachers must also communicate sensitively across cultural and linguistic differences and create an environment where students feel safe to speak and ask questions. The exam expects teachers to use communication strategically to promote engagement, clarify thinking, and advance learning for all students.

items: Communicate content clearly and accurately at students' developmental level.
Use varied questioning, adequate wait time, and equitable distribution of questions.
Check for understanding frequently and adjust based on responses.
Employ examples, analogies, models, and visuals to make ideas accessible.
Promote student-to-student discourse and elaborated, respectful responses.
Use nonverbal cues—tone, proximity, gestures—to support communication and management.
Listen actively and communicate sensitively across cultural and linguistic differences.

blocks.text: Teachers are responsible for developing students' ability to think critically, reason, and solve problems, not merely recall facts. This means designing instruction that engages higher-order thinking—analysis, evaluation, synthesis, and creation—often framed by taxonomies such as Bloom's. Teachers pose open-ended, thought-provoking questions and problems, encourage multiple approaches and solutions, and ask students to justify reasoning with evidence. Inquiry-based, problem-based, and project-based learning give students authentic contexts to investigate, hypothesize, and apply knowledge. Teachers model thinking processes, teach metacognitive strategies, and prompt reflection so students learn how to learn. Connecting content to real-world situations increases relevance and motivation while requiring transfer of skills. Effective teachers also encourage creativity, curiosity, and intellectual risk-taking, treating errors as learning opportunities. They scaffold complex tasks and gradually release responsibility so students become independent thinkers. The exam emphasizes that teachers should structure learning so students actively construct understanding, evaluate information, and apply skills to novel problems, building the reasoning capacities students need beyond school.

items: Promote higher-order thinking: analysis, evaluation, synthesis, and creation.
Use open-ended questions and problems that invite multiple approaches.
Require students to justify reasoning with evidence.
Apply inquiry-, problem-, and project-based learning in authentic contexts.
Model thinking and teach metacognitive, self-regulation strategies.
Connect content to real-world situations to support transfer and motivation.
Encourage creativity, curiosity, and productive risk-taking; treat errors as learning.

topics.title: Technology to Enhance Teaching and Learning

blocks.text: Teachers integrate technology purposefully to enhance instruction, engagement, and learning, aligning tools with objectives rather than using technology for its own sake. Effective integration supports differentiation, collaboration, creativity, communication, and access to information, and can help students develop digital literacy needed for life and work. Teachers select appropriate digital resources, evaluate their quality and credibility, and use them to deepen understanding—through simulations, multimedia, productivity tools, and adaptive software. Technology also enables formative assessment, immediate feedback, and individualized practice. Teachers must address equitable access, accommodate diverse learners, and ensure tools are developmentally appropriate. Critically, teachers model and teach responsible, safe, ethical, and legal use of technology—digital citizenship—including privacy, copyright, and respectful online behavior. They guard student data and supervise online activity. The exam expects teachers to use technology to extend what is possible in the classroom, foster student-centered learning, and prepare students to be capable, responsible digital citizens, while always grounding tech choices in sound instructional goals.

items: Integrate technology to serve clear instructional objectives, not for novelty.
Use digital tools to differentiate, engage, collaborate, and provide feedback.
Evaluate digital resources for quality, accuracy, and credibility.
Teach digital literacy and responsible, safe, ethical use (digital citizenship).
Address equitable access and accommodate diverse learners.
Protect student privacy and data and supervise online activity.
Leverage technology for adaptive practice, simulations, and individualized learning.

blocks.text: During instruction, teachers continuously monitor student understanding and adjust teaching in response—an ongoing cycle of assessing, interpreting, and acting. They use frequent formative checks—questioning, observation, exit tickets, quick writes, and student work—to gauge progress in real time and identify who needs reteaching, enrichment, or different strategies. Responsive teaching means modifying pacing, grouping, examples, or methods when evidence shows students are confused or ready to advance. Feedback is central: effective feedback is specific, timely, descriptive, and focused on the task and how to improve, guiding students toward goals rather than simply labeling work right or wrong. Teachers help students understand criteria for success and use feedback to revise and grow. They also promote student self-monitoring and reflection, building independence. Data from ongoing assessment informs both immediate adjustments and longer-term planning. The exam emphasizes the tight, dynamic link between assessment and instruction: teachers must gather evidence of learning constantly and use it to make instructional decisions that move every student forward.

items: Continuously monitor understanding with frequent formative checks during lessons.
Adjust pacing, grouping, methods, and examples based on real-time evidence.
Identify who needs reteaching, support, or enrichment and respond accordingly.
Give feedback that is specific, timely, descriptive, and improvement-focused.
Clarify success criteria so students can use feedback to revise and grow.
Foster student self-monitoring, reflection, and goal-setting.
Use assessment data to inform both immediate and long-term instructional decisions.

blocks.text: Questioning is one of a teacher's most powerful instructional tools, shaping the depth of thinking and the breadth of participation. Effective questioning blends lower-order questions (recall, comprehension) with higher-order, open-ended questions (analysis, evaluation, synthesis) that have multiple valid responses and require justification. Convergent questions seek a single correct answer; divergent questions invite varied thinking. To engage all learners, teachers use strategies such as cold calling thoughtfully, randomizing responders, no-hands questioning, think-pair-share, and posing the question before naming a student so everyone prepares an answer. Wait time, researched by Mary Budd Rowe, is critical: after asking a question, pausing at least three to five seconds (Wait Time I) and pausing again after a student responds (Wait Time II) dramatically improves the length, quality, and number of student responses, and increases participation from reluctant students. Teachers should also probe and scaffold responses rather than accepting only correct answers, redirecting and prompting to extend thinking. For the PPR exam, recognize that purposeful, higher-order questions, equitable response strategies, and adequate wait time promote deeper engagement, surface misconceptions, and signal high expectations that every student can think and contribute.

items: Balance lower-order recall with higher-order, open-ended questions.
Convergent questions seek one answer; divergent questions invite many.
Pose the question before naming a responder so all students think.
Wait Time I: pause 3-5 seconds after asking before calling on anyone.
Wait Time II: pause after a response to allow elaboration.
Adequate wait time increases response quality and participation.
Probe, prompt, and redirect to extend and deepen thinking.

blocks.text: Meaningful technology integration enhances learning rather than merely digitizing old practices. Two frameworks guide thoughtful use. The SAMR model (Puentedura) describes four levels of integration: Substitution (tech replaces a tool with no functional change, e.g., typing instead of handwriting), Augmentation (tech replaces a tool with functional improvement, e.g., a document with spellcheck and comments), Modification (tech allows significant task redesign, e.g., collaborative real-time editing), and Redefinition (tech enables previously impossible tasks, e.g., publishing to a global audience or co-creating with peers worldwide). The lower levels enhance tasks; the upper levels transform them. The TPACK framework emphasizes the integration of three knowledge domains: Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge. Effective teaching lives where all three overlap, using the right tool, with the right teaching method, for the right content. Technology should serve clear learning objectives, not exist for novelty. Teachers must also weigh equity and access, digital citizenship, safety, and accessibility for students with disabilities. For the PPR exam, recognize that strong integration is purposeful and learning-driven, that the goal is to reach transformative (Modification/Redefinition) uses when appropriate, and that pedagogy and content, not the device, lead the decision.

items: SAMR levels: Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition.
Substitution/Augmentation enhance; Modification/Redefinition transform learning.
TPACK overlaps Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge.
Technology should serve clear objectives, not novelty.
Aim for transformative uses (redesign or previously impossible tasks).
Address equity, access, safety, and digital citizenship.
Pedagogy and content lead tool selection, not the device.

blocks.text: Feedback is among the highest-impact influences on achievement, but only when it is timely, specific, and actionable. Effective feedback is descriptive rather than evaluative, it tells students what they did, how it compares to the goal, and what to do next, instead of simply assigning a grade or saying 'good job.' Hattie and Timperley frame feedback around three questions: Where am I going? (the goal and success criteria), How am I going? (current progress), and Where to next? (next steps to close the gap). Strong feedback is tied to clear learning targets, focuses on the task and process rather than the person, and is given while students can still act on it. Praise directed at effort and strategy ('feed-forward') supports a growth mindset, whereas praise of fixed ability can reduce risk-taking. Teachers balance teacher feedback with peer feedback and student self-assessment, building learners' capacity to monitor their own work. Feedback should be manageable, prioritizing one or two key improvements rather than overwhelming students with corrections. For the PPR exam, recognize that effective feedback is specific, criterion-referenced, timely, and oriented toward improvement, and that it forms a loop with formative assessment to advance learning.

items: Effective feedback is specific, timely, and actionable, not just a grade.
Hattie's three questions: Where going? How going? Where next?
Focus on the task and process, not the person's traits.
Give feedback while students can still act on it.
Praise effort and strategy to support a growth mindset.
Use peer feedback and self-assessment to build self-monitoring.
Prioritize one or two improvements rather than overwhelming students.

blocks.text: Response to Intervention (RTI) and the broader Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS) are frameworks for providing increasingly intensive, data-driven help to students who struggle academically or behaviorally, before referring them for special education. The model uses tiers. Tier 1 is high-quality, differentiated core instruction delivered to all students in the general classroom, typically meeting the needs of roughly 80 percent. Tier 2 provides targeted, supplemental support, often in small groups, for students who need more (around 15 percent). Tier 3 offers intensive, individualized intervention for the few students (about 5 percent) with the greatest needs. MTSS expands RTI beyond academics to include behavior (integrating PBIS) and the whole child. Central to the framework is universal screening to identify needs early, ongoing progress monitoring to gauge whether interventions are working, and data-based decision-making to adjust or intensify support. Crucially, RTI/MTSS is preventive and does not replace special education evaluation, persistent lack of response despite quality intervention can trigger a referral. For the PPR exam, recognize that interventions must be evidence-based, that decisions rest on data, that support increases in intensity by tier, and that the goal is early, layered help within general education.

items: RTI/MTSS provides tiered, data-driven support before special education referral.
Tier 1: quality core instruction for all (~80%).
Tier 2: targeted supplemental support, often small-group (~15%).
Tier 3: intensive, individualized intervention (~5%).
MTSS includes behavior (PBIS) and the whole child, not just academics.
Universal screening and progress monitoring drive decisions.
Lack of response to quality intervention may trigger a referral.

blocks.text: Inquiry and problem-based learning shift students from passive recipients to active investigators who construct understanding by grappling with authentic questions and real-world problems. Grounded in constructivism, these approaches hold that durable knowledge is built, not transmitted. In inquiry, students pose questions, gather and analyze evidence, and draw conclusions, mirroring how disciplines actually generate knowledge. Problem-based learning anchors a unit in a complex, often messy challenge that has no single tidy answer, driving students to research, collaborate, and apply content in service of a solution. The teacher's role transforms from lecturer to facilitator—designing rich problems, asking probing questions, providing resources, and scaffolding without simply handing over answers. Productive struggle is intentional: confusion and revision are signs of learning, not failure. Effective implementation still demands structure; pure discovery without guidance can overload novices, so teachers calibrate support to learners' expertise, front-loading foundational knowledge before turning students loose. These methods build critical thinking, transfer, collaboration, and motivation because the work is purposeful and student-driven. Assessment shifts toward processes and products—models, arguments, prototypes—judged with clear rubrics. Inquiry also raises engagement by honoring curiosity and giving students voice and choice. For the EC-12 teacher, the skill lies in balancing open exploration with the scaffolding and explicit instruction that keep all learners progressing toward rigorous standards.

items: Rooted in constructivism: students build understanding by investigating authentic questions and problems.
Inquiry follows a question-evidence-conclusion cycle that mirrors how disciplines create knowledge.
Problem-based learning anchors units in complex, real-world challenges with no single tidy answer.
The teacher becomes a facilitator—designing problems, probing, and scaffolding without handing over answers.
Productive struggle is intentional; confusion and revision signal learning, not failure.
Calibrate guidance to expertise—novices need foundational knowledge before fully open discovery.
Assess processes and products (models, arguments, prototypes) with clear rubrics, and leverage student voice and choice.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Digital Citizenship & Assistive Technology

blocks.text: Technology in the EC-12 classroom serves two intertwined purposes: preparing students to participate responsibly in a digital world and removing barriers so every learner can access the curriculum. Digital citizenship is the set of skills and dispositions students need to use technology safely, ethically, and productively—protecting privacy, recognizing their digital footprint, evaluating online sources critically, respecting intellectual property to avoid plagiarism, and treating others with respect to prevent cyberbullying. Teachers model these behaviors, teach them explicitly, and reinforce safe practices aligned with school acceptable-use policies and laws governing student data. Effective technology integration is not about flashy tools but about purposeful use that deepens learning; frameworks like SAMR remind teachers to move beyond mere substitution toward redefining tasks in ways impossible without technology. Assistive technology, meanwhile, ranges from low-tech supports such as pencil grips and visual schedules to high-tech tools like text-to-speech, speech-to-text, screen readers, and augmentative communication devices. For students with disabilities, these supports may be required accommodations documented in an IEP or 504 plan, and they can be transformative for access and independence. Universal Design for Learning extends the spirit further, offering multiple means of representation, engagement, and expression so flexible options benefit all students. The skilled teacher selects tools intentionally, ensures equitable access, and keeps the focus on learning goals rather than the technology itself.

items: Digital citizenship covers safety, privacy, digital footprint, source evaluation, intellectual property, and respectful online conduct.
Teach and model ethical technology use aligned with acceptable-use policies and student-data laws.
Integrate technology purposefully to deepen learning—move beyond substitution toward redefinition (e.g., SAMR).
Assistive technology spans low-tech (visual schedules, grips) to high-tech (text-to-speech, AAC devices).
AT may be a required accommodation in a student's IEP or 504 plan, supporting access and independence.
Universal Design for Learning provides multiple means of representation, engagement, and expression for all learners.
