blocks.text: Checks for understanding are the moment-to-moment formative assessments that tell a teacher whether learning is actually happening while there is still time to act. Unlike summative tests that certify mastery after instruction, these quick checks are woven throughout a lesson to surface misconceptions, gauge readiness to move on, and guide real-time adjustments. The hallmark of an effective check is that it gathers evidence from all students, not just the few who volunteer. Techniques such as cold call, total-participation responses, whiteboards, exit tickets, hinge questions, think-pair-share, and digital polling make every learner's thinking visible. A well-designed hinge question, placed at a pivot point, reveals whether the class is ready to proceed because wrong answers map to specific misconceptions. The point is not merely collecting data but using it: a teacher who finds widespread confusion reteaches, models again, or adjusts grouping, while strong understanding signals it is safe to advance or extend. Checks should align tightly to the objective and target the cognitive level intended. They also fuel feedback that is timely, specific, and actionable, helping students close the gap between current and desired performance. When checks are frequent, low-stakes, and responsive, they keep instruction adaptive and prevent the common trap of teaching to the front row while gaps quietly widen across the room.

items: Checks for understanding are formative—they inform instruction in real time, not certify mastery.
Gather evidence from ALL students (whiteboards, total-participation techniques, exit tickets), not just volunteers.
Use hinge questions at pivot points where wrong answers reveal specific misconceptions.
The data must drive action: reteach, remodel, or regroup on confusion; advance or extend on mastery.
Align each check to the objective and the intended cognitive level.
Pair checks with timely, specific, actionable feedback that helps students close performance gaps.
Keep checks frequent and low-stakes to stay adaptive and avoid teaching only to the front row.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Bloom's & Webb's Depth of Knowledge

blocks.text: Bloom's Taxonomy and Webb's Depth of Knowledge are complementary frameworks for raising cognitive rigor, but they measure different things. The revised Bloom's Taxonomy classifies the type of thinking verb a task demands across six levels: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create. It is useful for varying question types and ensuring students move beyond recall. Webb's Depth of Knowledge, by contrast, measures the complexity and depth of mental processing a task requires, across four levels: DOK 1 recall and reproduction, DOK 2 skills and concepts, DOK 3 strategic thinking and reasoning, and DOK 4 extended thinking over time. A key insight is that a high Bloom's verb does not guarantee high DOK. 'Analyze' a familiar, fully scaffolded example may be simpler than a DOK 3 task asking students to justify a conclusion with evidence amid ambiguity. Conversely, the same verb can sit at different depths depending on the task's novelty, the number of steps, and how much reasoning students must supply. Skilled teachers plan for a balance, ensuring assessments include genuinely complex items and that the cognitive demand matches the learning goal. On the PPR, expect items asking you to identify a question's level, increase rigor, or align assessment demand to objectives; the strongest answers push toward authentic reasoning, not just harder vocabulary.

items: Bloom's classifies the type of thinking; DOK measures the depth and complexity of processing.
Bloom's levels: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create.
DOK levels: recall (1), skills/concepts (2), strategic thinking (3), extended thinking (4).
A high Bloom's verb does not automatically mean high DOK; context and novelty matter.
Depth rises with task novelty, multiple steps, ambiguity, and the reasoning students must supply.
Plan a balance of levels and match cognitive demand to the learning objective.
On exam items, increase rigor through authentic reasoning, not merely harder vocabulary.

blocks.text: Cooperative learning is more than grouping students and hoping they collaborate; it is a deliberately structured approach that makes the group's success depend on every member's learning. Johnson and Johnson identified five essential elements that distinguish genuine cooperative learning from mere group work. Positive interdependence means students sink or swim together, often engineered through shared goals, divided roles, or interlocking resources. Individual accountability ensures each student is responsible for their own learning, preventing 'free riders' and 'social loafing,' typically by assessing individuals or randomly calling on any member. Promotive (face-to-face) interaction has students explaining, questioning, and encouraging one another. Interpersonal and small-group skills, such as turn-taking, active listening, and conflict resolution, must be taught, not assumed. Group processing asks teams to reflect on how well they worked and how to improve. Named structures operationalize these elements: Think-Pair-Share gives processing time before sharing; Jigsaw makes each student an 'expert' whose piece the group needs; Numbered Heads Together builds accountability because any number may be called. The teacher's role shifts to designing tasks, teaching social skills, monitoring, and intervening only as needed. On the PPR, cooperative learning items reward answers that build in both positive interdependence and individual accountability, the two non-negotiable elements that separate effective cooperative learning from chaotic or inequitable group work.

items: Cooperative learning is structured so the group's success depends on each member's learning.
Five elements: positive interdependence, individual accountability, promotive interaction, social skills, group processing.
Positive interdependence is built through shared goals, divided roles, or interlocking resources.
Individual accountability prevents free-riders by assessing or calling on individuals.
Social skills like listening, turn-taking, and conflict resolution must be explicitly taught.
Structures: Think-Pair-Share, Jigsaw, and Numbered Heads Together operationalize the elements.
Strong exam answers ensure both interdependence and accountability, not just seating in groups.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Using Data to Drive Instruction

blocks.text: Data-driven instruction is the disciplined cycle of gathering evidence about student learning and using it to make timely teaching decisions, rather than assessing only to assign grades. Teachers draw on multiple data types: diagnostic assessments reveal prior knowledge and gaps before a unit, formative assessments monitor learning in progress, and summative assessments evaluate mastery at the end. The real power lies in formative data, because it is actionable while there is still time to adjust. The cycle runs continuously: collect evidence (exit tickets, quizzes, observations, work samples), analyze it to find patterns and group students by need, then act by reteaching, regrouping, accelerating, or differentiating. Effective teachers disaggregate data to see which students or which standards need attention, and they look for trends across the class rather than fixating on a single score. Data also drives flexible grouping, where students move among groups as their needs change, and it informs feedback that tells learners exactly what to do next. Crucially, assessment results should loop back to instruction and to students themselves, who can use the information to set goals and self-monitor. On the PPR, watch for scenarios where a teacher notices a pattern of errors; the best responses analyze the cause, then adjust instruction or grouping, rather than simply moving on or re-teaching identically to the whole class.

items: Data-driven instruction uses assessment evidence to make teaching decisions, not just to assign grades.
Diagnostic data finds gaps before a unit; formative monitors during; summative evaluates at the end.
Formative data is the most actionable because there is still time to adjust instruction.
Run a continuous cycle: collect evidence, analyze patterns, then act by reteaching or regrouping.
Disaggregate results to identify which students and which standards need attention.
Use data for flexible grouping and for feedback that tells students their next step.
On exam items, analyze the cause of error patterns and adjust, rather than reteaching identically.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Discussion Protocols & Wait Time

blocks.text: Rich classroom discussion deepens thinking, but it requires deliberate structures so that talk is equitable and rigorous rather than dominated by a few quick responders. Wait time, the pause a teacher leaves after asking a question and again after a student responds, is one of the most powerful, research-supported moves. Extending that pause to several seconds increases the length and quality of responses, draws in more students, and raises the cognitive level of answers, especially for students who process more deliberately or are learning English. Discussion protocols add structure that ensures participation: Think-Pair-Share lets students rehearse ideas before speaking; cold-calling paired with prior partner talk spreads accountability without ambushing; structured formats such as Socratic seminars, fishbowls, and turn-and-talks distribute voice and model academic discourse. Teachers strengthen discussion by asking open-ended, higher-order questions, by using probing follow-ups that push for evidence and reasoning, and by encouraging student-to-student response rather than routing every comment through the teacher. On the PPR exam, the strongest answers favor strategies that maximize the number of students thinking and talking, build in processing time, and hold all learners accountable for reasoning. Avoid patterns where the teacher accepts the first hand or rushes to fill silence. Effective discourse also depends on a safe climate where errors are treated as learning opportunities, ensuring every student can contribute and learn from peers.

items: Wait time (pause after the question and after a response) increases response length, quality, and participation.
Extending wait time especially helps deliberate processors and emergent bilingual students reach higher-order answers.
Think-Pair-Share, turn-and-talks, fishbowls, and Socratic seminars structure equitable, rigorous talk.
Cold-call after partner talk to spread accountability without ambushing students.
Ask open-ended, higher-order questions and use probing follow-ups for evidence and reasoning.
Promote student-to-student discourse and a safe climate where errors are learning opportunities.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Choosing the Right EdTech Tool

blocks.text: Technology should serve the learning objective, never the reverse. The defining question when selecting an EdTech tool is whether it advances the specific TEKS-aligned goal better than a non-digital alternative, and whether it deepens thinking rather than merely digitizing low-level tasks. Frameworks such as SAMR (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) help teachers move beyond simply substituting a worksheet for a screen toward tasks that were previously impossible, such as collaborating with distant peers, analyzing live data, or creating multimedia products. The TPACK framework reminds teachers that strong choices integrate technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge together. Practical selection criteria include alignment to the objective, accessibility for all learners including those with disabilities and emergent bilinguals, student data privacy and compliance with district and legal requirements, equity of access to devices and connectivity, ease of use, and the quality of feedback the tool provides. Teachers must also plan for digital citizenship, safe and ethical online behavior, and have a backup plan when technology fails. On the PPR exam, the best answers choose tools because they enhance engagement, differentiation, collaboration, or higher-order thinking tied to a clear goal, and reject technology used merely for novelty or as a reward. Effective integration keeps the teacher as facilitator, monitors student work, and evaluates whether the tool actually improved learning outcomes.

items: Start with the objective: choose a tool only if it advances the TEKS-aligned goal better than a non-digital option.
Use SAMR to move from mere substitution toward tasks that redefine what learning is possible.
TPACK integrates technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge in effective tech decisions.
Vet tools for accessibility, data privacy/legal compliance, equity of access, usability, and feedback quality.
Teach digital citizenship and always have a backup plan for technology failures.
Reject tech used for novelty or reward; select it to deepen engagement, differentiation, and higher-order thinking.

blocks.text: Formative assessment is the ongoing, low-stakes gathering of evidence during learning so that teachers can adjust instruction and students can adjust their effort while there is still time to improve. Unlike summative assessment, which judges mastery after instruction, formative assessment is assessment for learning, not of learning, and its central purpose is feedback and responsive action. Effective techniques make student thinking visible quickly: exit tickets, whiteboards or response cards used by all students at once, cold-calling, thumbs-up checks, hinge questions, one-sentence summaries, and digital polling tools. The defining feature is the loop, the teacher collects evidence, interprets it, and then does something with it, whether reteaching, regrouping, providing targeted feedback, or moving on. Crucially, formative checks should sample the whole class rather than the few volunteers, so that decisions reflect all learners. High-quality feedback is timely, specific, and tied to criteria, telling students where they are relative to the goal and what to do next, rather than simply assigning a grade. Self-assessment and peer assessment, anchored to clear success criteria or rubrics, build student metacognition and ownership. On the PPR exam, the strongest answers select methods that check all students, occur during the lesson, and lead to an instructional adjustment. The wrong answer treats a quiz as merely a grade rather than as actionable information for both teacher and learner.

items: Formative assessment is ongoing, low-stakes evidence-gathering during learning, assessment for learning, not of it.
Techniques include exit tickets, all-student response cards, hinge questions, polling, and one-sentence summaries.
The essential loop: collect evidence, interpret it, then adjust instruction (reteach, regroup, or move on).
Sample the whole class, not just volunteers, so decisions reflect every learner.
Feedback should be timely, specific, and criteria-based, telling students what to do next rather than just a grade.
Peer and self-assessment against clear success criteria build metacognition and student ownership.

blocks.text: Questioning is among a teacher's most powerful instructional tools, yet much classroom questioning stays at the recall level. Higher-order questioning pushes students to analyze, evaluate, and create, the upper tiers of Bloom's revised taxonomy and the more demanding levels of Webb's Depth of Knowledge. Rather than asking only what happened, teachers ask why, how, what if, and what evidence supports a claim, prompting reasoning, justification, and synthesis. Skilled questioning is deliberate. Teachers plan key questions in advance, sequence them to build complexity, and embed them at pivotal points in a lesson. Wait time is essential: pausing three to five seconds after posing a question, and again after a student responds, dramatically increases the length, depth, and number of student answers. Equitable techniques, such as cold-calling, no-hands-up protocols, and randomized selection, distribute thinking across the whole class rather than rewarding the fastest few. Follow-up moves, including probing for evidence, asking students to elaborate, and redirecting questions to peers, sustain dialogue and surface misconceptions. Effective teachers also create a climate where wrong answers are treated as productive thinking opportunities. For the TExES, candidates connect higher-order questioning to critical thinking, formative assessment, differentiation, and rigorous, student-centered discourse aligned to learning objectives.

items: Higher-order questions target analysis, evaluation, and creation, moving beyond simple recall.
Use frameworks such as Bloom's revised taxonomy and Webb's Depth of Knowledge to plan questions of increasing rigor.
Plan and sequence key questions in advance rather than improvising at the lowest level.
Apply wait time after the question and after a student response to deepen and lengthen answers.
Distribute participation equitably with cold-calling, no-hands protocols, and random selection.
Use probing follow-ups (ask for evidence, elaboration, peer redirection) to sustain reasoning and reveal misconceptions.
Build a safe climate where errors become opportunities to examine thinking.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Universal Design for Learning (UDL)

blocks.text: Universal Design for Learning is a proactive framework for planning instruction that is accessible and challenging for the full range of learners from the outset, rather than retrofitting accommodations after the fact. Drawing on neuroscience, UDL recognizes that learners vary predictably in how they engage, perceive information, and express what they know, so flexibility should be built into the design. The framework organizes practice around three principles. Multiple means of engagement address the 'why' of learning by offering choice, relevance, and supports for sustaining effort and self-regulation, recognizing that motivation differs across students. Multiple means of representation address the 'what' by presenting content in varied formats, such as text, audio, visuals, and demonstrations, and by clarifying vocabulary and highlighting key ideas. Multiple means of action and expression address the 'how' by letting students demonstrate understanding through diverse products and by providing tools, scaffolds, and goal-setting supports. A central UDL idea is reducing barriers in the environment rather than locating deficits in the student. Well-designed options benefit everyone, not only students with disabilities, exemplifying the curb-cut effect. For the TExES, candidates connect UDL to differentiation, accessibility, equity, and inclusive instruction that anticipates learner variability during planning.

items: UDL is proactive design that builds accessibility and challenge in from the start, not after-the-fact accommodation.
Three principles: multiple means of engagement (the why), representation (the what), and action and expression (the how).
Engagement options provide choice, relevance, and supports for persistence and self-regulation.
Representation options present content in varied formats and clarify language and key concepts.
Action and expression options allow varied products and provide tools, scaffolds, and goal-setting.
Locate barriers in the environment or task design rather than viewing the student as deficient.
Flexible options benefit all learners (the curb-cut effect), supporting equity and differentiation.

blocks.text: Peer and self-assessment are formative practices that position students as active participants in evaluating learning rather than passive recipients of grades. In self-assessment, students judge their own work against clear criteria, reflect on strengths and gaps, and set goals for improvement. In peer assessment, students give and receive feedback from classmates using shared standards. Both build metacognition, the ability to monitor and regulate one's own learning, which research consistently links to higher achievement and greater independence. These practices depend on transparency: students need explicit success criteria, often through rubrics, checklists, or exemplars, so their judgments are accurate rather than arbitrary. Teachers must also teach feedback skills directly, modeling how to give specific, kind, and actionable comments and how to focus on the work rather than the person. Sentence stems, structured protocols, and anonymized samples help students practice safely. A common pitfall is treating these as grading shortcuts; their real power is formative, informing revision before final evaluation. Self- and peer assessment also increase ownership, motivation, and understanding of what quality looks like. The teacher remains responsible for validating judgments and ensuring fairness. For the TExES, candidates connect these strategies to formative assessment, metacognition, student-centered learning, feedback that advances growth, and clear communication of expectations.

items: Peer and self-assessment make students active evaluators, building metacognition and learner independence.
Both require explicit success criteria via rubrics, checklists, or exemplars to ensure accurate judgments.
Teach feedback skills directly: specific, kind, actionable, and focused on the work, not the person.
Use sentence stems, structured protocols, and anonymized samples to build the skill safely.
Keep the purpose formative, guiding revision before final evaluation rather than serving as a grading shortcut.
These practices raise ownership, motivation, and understanding of quality.
The teacher still validates judgments and ensures fairness and reliability.

sections.title: Fulfilling Professional Roles and Responsibilities
sections.summary: 22 lessons for Domain 4 (20% of the exam).

blocks.text: Teachers build strong, respectful partnerships with families and caregivers to support student learning and well-being. Research shows family involvement improves achievement, attendance, and behavior, so teachers communicate proactively, regularly, and in ways families can access. Effective communication is clear, positive, two-way, and culturally and linguistically responsive; teachers share both successes and concerns and invite family input. They keep families informed about goals, progress, expectations, and ways to support learning at home. Teachers conduct productive conferences, respond promptly to questions, and use multiple channels—notes, calls, digital platforms, meetings—to reach diverse families. They treat families as valued partners with important knowledge about their children and remain sensitive to varied family structures, cultures, languages, and circumstances. Teachers also connect families with school and community resources when appropriate, and maintain professionalism and confidentiality in all interactions. The exam emphasizes that teachers should initiate and sustain collaborative relationships with families, communicate respectfully and clearly, and engage families as allies in promoting each student's growth and success.

items: Family involvement improves achievement, attendance, and behavior.
Communicate proactively, regularly, positively, and in two directions.
Be culturally and linguistically responsive and respect diverse family structures.
Share goals, progress, and ways families can support learning at home.
Use multiple channels and conduct productive, respectful conferences.
Treat families as valued partners with knowledge about their children.
Connect families to resources and maintain professionalism and confidentiality.

blocks.text: Teaching is a collaborative profession that demands ongoing reflection and improvement. Effective teachers work productively with colleagues, administrators, specialists, and support staff—through professional learning communities, co-planning, mentoring, and team problem-solving—to improve instruction and support students. They contribute positively to the school community and seek and use feedback constructively. Reflective practice is essential: teachers regularly examine their own teaching, analyze results and student data, identify strengths and needs, and set goals for growth. They pursue meaningful professional development, stay current with research-based practices, and apply new learning to their classrooms. Teachers also collaborate to support students with special needs, contributing to processes such as intervention planning and individualized programs. Mentoring relationships and induction support help novice teachers develop. The exam emphasizes that effective educators are lifelong learners who take responsibility for their professional growth, engage collegially, reflect critically on practice, and continually refine their skills. Collaboration and reflection together strengthen both individual practice and the broader learning community for the benefit of students.

items: Collaborate with colleagues, specialists, and staff to improve instruction and support students.
Participate in professional learning communities and co-planning.
Engage in reflective practice: analyze teaching and data, set growth goals.
Seek, accept, and act on constructive feedback.
Pursue ongoing, research-based professional development and apply it.
Contribute positively to the school community and mentoring relationships.
Take personal responsibility as a lifelong learner and professional.

topics.title: Legal and Ethical Responsibilities of Texas Educators

blocks.text: Teachers must know and uphold the legal and ethical obligations that govern the profession in Texas. The Texas Educators' Code of Ethics sets standards for professional conduct toward the profession, the public, and students—prohibiting misconduct, dishonesty, and inappropriate relationships, and requiring fairness, integrity, and protection of students. Teachers are mandated reporters: they must report suspected child abuse or neglect promptly to the proper authorities, and failure to do so carries legal consequences. FERPA protects the privacy of student education records, limiting disclosure and granting rights to parents and eligible students. Teachers must understand special education law—IDEA, IEPs, least restrictive environment, and related due process—plus Section 504 protections, and their duty to provide appropriate services and accommodations. Other key areas include equal access, anti-discrimination, copyright, student safety and supervision, confidentiality, and appropriate use of authority. Teachers act in students' best interests, maintain professional boundaries, and follow district and state policies. The exam expects teachers to recognize legal requirements and ethical duties and apply them correctly to protect students' rights and well-being.

items: The Texas Educators' Code of Ethics governs conduct toward students, public, and profession.
Teachers are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse or neglect—report promptly.
FERPA protects student record privacy and grants rights to parents/eligible students.
IDEA governs special education: IEPs, least restrictive environment, and due process.
Section 504 provides accommodations for students with disabilities.
Maintain confidentiality, professional boundaries, and student safety and supervision.
Act in students' best interests and follow district, state, and federal law.

topics.title: Special Education Law: IDEA, IEP, LRE & 504

blocks.text: Federal law guarantees students with disabilities access to education, and teachers must know the core provisions. The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) ensures a Free Appropriate Public Education (FAPE) for eligible students and requires an Individualized Education Program (IEP), a legally binding plan developed by a team that includes parents, general and special educators, and a district representative. The IEP specifies present levels, measurable goals, services, accommodations, and how progress is measured. IDEA mandates the Least Restrictive Environment (LRE), meaning students must be educated with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate, with removal only when the general setting with supports cannot meet their needs. Key IDEA principles also include nondiscriminatory evaluation, procedural due process, and parent participation. Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is a civil-rights law with broader eligibility: it protects any student with a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, providing accommodations through a 504 plan even when the student does not qualify under IDEA. Thus all IDEA students are covered, but many 504 students are not IDEA-eligible. For the PPR exam, know FAPE, LRE, the IEP team and components, parent rights, and the distinction between IDEA services and 504 accommodations.

items: IDEA guarantees FAPE for eligible students with disabilities.
The IEP is a legally binding plan with goals, services, and accommodations.
The IEP team includes parents, general and special educators, and a district rep.
LRE: educate with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate.
IDEA requires nondiscriminatory evaluation and procedural due process.
Section 504 has broader eligibility and provides accommodations via a 504 plan.
All IDEA students are protected, but many 504 students are not IDEA-eligible.

topics.title: The Texas Educators' Code of Ethics

blocks.text: The Texas Educators' Code of Ethics, adopted by the State Board for Educator Certification (SBEC), sets professional standards that govern educator conduct and is heavily tested on the PPR exam. It is organized into three categories: professional ethical conduct, practices, and performance; ethical conduct toward professional colleagues; and ethical conduct toward students. The first addresses integrity in handling funds, records, and credentials, prohibiting misrepresentation, misappropriation of resources, and falsifying records. The second governs relationships with colleagues, prohibiting discrimination, coercion, retaliation, and the disclosure of confidential colleague information without cause, while protecting reporting rights. The third, most critical for daily practice, focuses on students: educators must not reveal confidential student information unless legally required, must not knowingly treat a student in a manner that adversely affects learning, physical health, mental health, or safety, must not exploit a professional relationship for personal advantage, and must avoid inappropriate communication or relationships with students, including through electronic media and social networking. Across all categories, the code emphasizes honesty, fairness, professional boundaries, and the welfare of students. For the PPR exam, recognize that ethical questions hinge on student safety, confidentiality, fairness, appropriate boundaries, and reporting obligations, and that the standard is always the student's best interest.

items: Adopted by SBEC; governs all Texas educators' professional conduct.
Three categories: professional conduct, conduct toward colleagues, conduct toward students.
Prohibits falsifying records and misusing or misappropriating resources.
Bars discrimination, coercion, and retaliation against colleagues.
Protects student confidentiality unless disclosure is legally required.
Forbids harming students or exploiting professional relationships.
Prohibits inappropriate communication, including via social media and electronic media.

blocks.text: The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) is a federal law protecting the privacy of student education records, and educators must handle records with care. FERPA gives parents the right to inspect and review their child's education records, to request corrections of inaccurate information, and to control the disclosure of personally identifiable information. These rights transfer to the student at age 18 or upon entering postsecondary education (the 'eligible student'). Generally, schools must obtain written consent before releasing records, but FERPA permits disclosure without consent in specific situations: to school officials with a legitimate educational interest, to another school where the student is enrolling, for health and safety emergencies, and in response to certain legal orders. 'Directory information' (such as name or grade level) may be released unless a parent opts out. In daily practice, confidentiality means not discussing a student's grades, behavior, disability, or family circumstances with unauthorized people, including in hallways, social media, or with other parents. Teachers should share student information only with colleagues who have a legitimate educational need. For the PPR exam, recognize parents' and eligible students' rights, the limited exceptions for disclosure without consent, and the everyday duty to protect sensitive student information professionally and discreetly.

blocks.text: In Texas, every educator is a mandated reporter, and this duty is both a legal and an ethical obligation tested on the PPR exam. Under the Texas Family Code, any person who suspects that a child has been or may be abused or neglected must make a report, and professionals such as teachers face a stricter standard. The report must be made promptly, within 48 hours of first suspecting abuse, and professionals may not delegate the duty to a supervisor or principal; the individual who suspects abuse must report personally. Reports go to the Department of Family and Protective Services (DFPS) or to law enforcement, and the reporter need not have proof, only a reasonable cause or suspicion. Teachers do not investigate; their role is to recognize warning signs and report. The law protects good-faith reporters from civil or criminal liability and keeps reporter identity confidential, while knowingly failing to report is a criminal offense. Importantly, a teacher cannot be relieved of this duty by school policy that requires reporting only to an administrator. For the PPR exam, remember the 48-hour timeline, the personal and non-delegable nature of the duty, the standard of reasonable suspicion rather than proof, and that protecting the child's safety always comes first.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Working with the ARD Committee

blocks.text: In Texas, the Admission, Review, and Dismissal (ARD) committee is the state's version of the IEP team and the legal decision-making body for students receiving special education under IDEA. The general education teacher is a required member because they bring essential knowledge of grade-level curriculum, classroom expectations, and the student's day-to-day performance among peers. The committee determines eligibility, develops and reviews the individualized education program, sets measurable annual goals, decides placement in the least restrictive environment, and identifies accommodations, modifications, and related services. A core principle is the least restrictive environment: students are educated with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate, with removal justified only when the nature of the disability prevents satisfactory progress with supplementary aids. Parents are equal partners with rights to participate, consent, receive notice, and exercise procedural safeguards, including dispute resolution. The general education teacher contributes data on progress, suggests strategies that work, and—critically—must implement the IEP's accommodations and modifications with fidelity once it is finalized; failure to do so is a legal compliance issue. Accommodations change how a student accesses content without altering expectations, while modifications change what is expected. Teachers should understand the difference, keep documentation, and communicate concerns through the process. Effective collaboration among general and special educators, related-service providers, administrators, and families produces a plan that genuinely supports the student's access and progress.

blocks.text: Section 504 and IDEA are two distinct federal laws that protect students with disabilities, and teachers must understand how they differ to serve students correctly. IDEA, the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, is special education law: it provides services to students who fall within specific disability categories and who, because of that disability, need specially designed instruction. Eligible students receive an individualized education program developed by the ARD/IEP team, with detailed goals, services, procedural safeguards, and funding attached. Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is broader and is a civil-rights antidiscrimination statute. It covers any student with a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity—a wider net that includes conditions like diabetes, severe allergies, ADHD, or anxiety that may not require specialized instruction but do require accommodations for equal access. A 504 plan typically lists accommodations rather than specialized instruction and goals. Both laws guarantee a free appropriate public education and protect against discrimination, but IDEA carries more comprehensive procedural protections and funding. A helpful way to remember the relationship: students eligible under IDEA are also protected by 504, but many 504 students do not qualify under IDEA. Teachers are legally responsible for implementing the accommodations in either plan with fidelity, documenting their use, and communicating with families and the support team about effectiveness and concerns.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Professional Boundaries & Social Media

blocks.text: Maintaining professional boundaries is a cornerstone of educator ethics and a frequent focus of PPR scenarios, because the teacher-student relationship carries an inherent power imbalance that must never be exploited. The Texas Educators' Code of Ethics sets clear expectations: teachers protect students from harm, avoid inappropriate relationships, refrain from soliciting or engaging in romantic or otherwise improper contact, and never misuse their position. Boundaries extend to communication—school-sanctioned channels should be used for student contact rather than personal phone numbers, private messaging, or personal social media accounts that blur professional lines. On social media, educators must assume that anything they post is public and permanent; content that is unprofessional, that disparages students or colleagues, that reveals confidential student information, or that undermines public trust can lead to disciplinary action even when posted off duty. Confidentiality is paramount: student records, performance, and personal circumstances are protected, and discussing identifiable students online or in public violates both ethics and privacy law. Sound practice includes keeping interactions transparent and observable, documenting concerns, avoiding gifts or favoritism that signal special relationships, and immediately reporting suspected abuse as a mandated reporter. When in doubt, teachers ask whether a behavior would withstand public scrutiny and serve the student's best interest. Upholding these boundaries protects students, preserves trust, and safeguards the educator's career and credibility.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Reflective Practice & Action Research

blocks.text: Reflective practice is the engine of continuous professional growth, transforming experience into improved teaching rather than letting it accumulate as mere routine. A reflective teacher systematically examines their own decisions, instruction, and student outcomes, asking not just what happened but why and what to do differently. This reflection operates on multiple timescales: reflection-in-action adjusts a lesson in the moment when students are confused, while reflection-on-action analyzes after the fact, often using student work, assessment data, and evidence of impact. The cycle is iterative—plan, act, observe, reflect, and refine—turning each lesson into a source of insight. Action research formalizes this stance: the teacher identifies a genuine problem of practice, poses a focused question, gathers and analyzes classroom data, implements a change, and evaluates its effect on student learning, then shares findings and repeats. This positions the teacher as an investigator of their own practice, grounding decisions in evidence rather than habit or assumption. Reflective educators also seek feedback through peer observation, mentoring, professional learning communities, and ongoing professional development, recognizing that growth is collaborative and lifelong. They use data to inform goals and view setbacks as information rather than failure. For the EC-12 teacher, this disposition—curious, self-critical, evidence-driven, and committed to improvement—sustains effectiveness over a career and models for students the very habits of learning the profession seeks to instill.

topics.title: Deep Dive: The IEP Process Step by Step

blocks.text: The Individualized Education Program process is the legal and instructional framework under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) for serving students with disabilities. It begins with identification: a child is referred, often after pre-referral interventions in general education fail to close the gap. With informed parental consent, a multidisciplinary team conducts a comprehensive, nondiscriminatory evaluation to determine whether the child has a qualifying disability and needs special education. If eligible, the IEP team, which must include the parents, a general education teacher, a special education teacher, an agency representative, someone who can interpret evaluation results, and when appropriate the student, develops the IEP. The document specifies the student's present levels of performance, measurable annual goals, the special education and related services to be provided, accommodations and modifications, and how progress will be measured. Two principles govern placement: the least restrictive environment, meaning students learn with nondisabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate, and the provision of a free appropriate public education. The IEP is reviewed at least annually and the student is reevaluated at least every three years. Parents hold procedural safeguards, including the right to participate, consent, access records, and pursue due process. On the PPR, the strongest answers honor parent involvement, the LRE mandate, and individualized, data-based decision-making over one-size-fits-all placements.

blocks.text: The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) is the federal law protecting the privacy of student education records, and it shapes daily decisions about what teachers may share and with whom. Education records are records directly related to a student and maintained by the school. FERPA grants parents specific rights: to inspect and review their child's records, to request corrections of inaccurate or misleading information, and to control the disclosure of personally identifiable information. These rights transfer to the student upon turning eighteen or enrolling in postsecondary education, at which point the student becomes an 'eligible student.' Generally, schools must obtain written consent before disclosing records, but FERPA permits disclosure without consent in defined situations, most importantly to school officials with a legitimate educational interest, meaning staff who need the information to do their jobs. 'Directory information' such as name or grade level may be released unless a parent has opted out. In practice, FERPA means a teacher does not post grades by name or student ID, does not discuss a child's performance with another parent, returns graded work discreetly, and shares records only with colleagues who have a genuine need to know. On the PPR, FERPA scenarios reward answers that protect confidentiality, route information appropriately, and obtain consent before disclosing records to outside parties or unauthorized individuals.

blocks.text: Co-teaching pairs two certified educators, frequently a general education teacher and a special education teacher, who share planning, instruction, and assessment for a blended group of students in the same classroom. Done well, it expands access to the general curriculum within the least restrictive environment while providing specialized support. Six recognized models give teachers flexible options. In 'one teach, one observe,' one leads instruction while the other gathers specific data on students. In 'one teach, one assist,' one leads while the other circulates to help; this is easy but, if overused, can relegate the specialist to an aide role. 'Station teaching' divides content into stations through which students rotate, with each teacher owning content. 'Parallel teaching' splits the class in half, with both teachers teaching the same material simultaneously to smaller groups, lowering the student-teacher ratio. 'Alternative teaching' pulls a small group aside for reteaching, preteaching, or enrichment while the larger group continues. 'Team teaching' has both educators sharing the lead fluidly, finishing each other's points like a true tag team. The choice depends on the lesson goal, student needs, and teacher familiarity. The strongest co-teaching rests on shared parity, joint planning time, and mutual respect. On the PPR, the best answers treat both teachers as equal professionals and match the model to the specific instructional purpose.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Parent Conferences That Work

blocks.text: A productive parent-teacher conference treats the family as a partner in the child's education, not an audience for a verdict. Preparation drives success: the teacher gathers concrete evidence such as work samples, assessment data, and behavior notes, and decides on two or three priorities rather than overwhelming the family with everything. The tone should be collaborative and strengths-based, opening with something genuine and positive about the child to build trust before discussing concerns. Effective communication means using plain language free of educational jargon and acronyms, listening as much as talking, and inviting the parent's perspective with open questions, since families hold knowledge about the child the teacher lacks. Cultural responsiveness matters: teachers honor diverse family structures, values, and communication norms, and arrange qualified interpreters rather than relying on the student or a sibling to translate sensitive information. The conference should produce a concrete, shared action plan with specific next steps for home and school and a way to follow up, turning conversation into partnership. Confidentiality is essential; discussions about one child must never reference other students. On the PPR, conference scenarios reward answers that are proactive, respectful, two-way, and solution-focused: contacting families early with good news and concerns, framing problems as shared challenges, and building a plan together rather than assigning blame or simply delivering instructions.

items: Approach families as partners; prepare with concrete evidence and two or three clear priorities.
Open with genuine positives and use a collaborative, strengths-based tone to build trust.
Communicate in plain language without jargon, and listen as much as you talk.
Invite the parent's perspective; families hold knowledge about the child the teacher lacks.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Mandatory Reporting Step by Step

blocks.text: In Texas, every teacher is a mandatory reporter and is legally required to report suspected child abuse or neglect. This duty is personal and non-delegable, which means the teacher who has the suspicion must make the report and cannot satisfy the law simply by telling a principal or counselor and assuming they will handle it. The standard for reporting is reasonable cause to believe or suspect; the teacher does not need proof, and it is not the teacher's job to investigate, interview the child at length, or determine guilt. Reports must be made promptly, generally within 48 hours, to the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services through its abuse hotline or online portal, or to a law enforcement agency. If a child is in immediate danger, contact law enforcement first. Reports made in good faith are confidential and grant the reporter immunity from civil or criminal liability, while knowingly failing to report is a crime. On the PPR exam, the defensible answer always reports directly to the proper authorities, acts promptly, and does not delay to gather evidence or wait for permission. Teachers should know their campus procedures but understand that internal reporting does not replace the legal report. Documentation of factual observations, not conclusions, is appropriate. Protecting the child's safety and following the law take precedence over fear of being wrong.

blocks.text: Paraprofessionals, also called teacher aides or instructional assistants, support instruction under the direction of a certified teacher, and the teacher remains responsible for planning, instruction, assessment, and overall decision-making. A productive partnership begins with clear roles: the teacher designs the lesson and learning goals, while the paraprofessional helps implement support such as reinforcing skills with small groups, assisting individual students, preparing materials, monitoring behavior, or providing accommodations specified in a student's IEP or 504 plan. Effective collaboration depends on communication, the teacher should share objectives, expectations, and routines, provide guidance and feedback, and respect the paraprofessional's observations and rapport with students. Boundaries matter: paraprofessionals generally should not be solely responsible for designing instruction, making high-stakes assessment judgments, or handling confidential matters beyond their role, and they must follow the same confidentiality and ethics expectations regarding student information. In special education settings, paraprofessionals are frequent partners in delivering services, and the teacher must ensure they understand each student's plan while still leading the instructional program. On the PPR exam, strong answers position the teacher as the instructional leader who directs, supports, and communicates with the paraprofessional as a valued team member, rather than abdicating responsibility or treating the aide as a peer with equal instructional authority. Mutual respect, defined tasks, ongoing feedback, and shared commitment to students produce the best outcomes for learners.

Define clear roles: teacher designs lessons and goals; paraprofessional reinforces skills, assists students, and prepares materials.
Communicate objectives, routines, and expectations, and provide ongoing guidance and feedback.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Culturally Responsive Family Engagement

blocks.text: Families are essential partners in student learning, and engaging them effectively requires honoring the cultural, linguistic, and economic diversity of the community. Culturally responsive engagement treats families as assets with valuable knowledge about their children, rather than as deficits to be fixed, and it builds two-way, respectful communication rather than one-directional messages from school to home. Practical strategies include communicating in families' home languages through translation and interpreters, offering flexible meeting times and formats for working parents, choosing welcoming and accessible locations, and reaching out with positive news, not only problems. Teachers should learn about the community's values and avoid assumptions, recognizing that involvement may look different across cultures and that all forms, such as encouragement at home, are valuable even when families cannot attend events. Barriers to engagement, including language, work schedules, transportation, prior negative school experiences, or unfamiliarity with U.S. school systems, should be anticipated and reduced. On the PPR exam, the strongest answers proactively initiate respectful contact, use families' languages, frame parents as collaborators in their child's education, and avoid blaming families for low involvement. Teachers should connect families to resources, invite their input into decisions, and share concrete ways to support learning at home. Genuine partnership rests on trust, cultural humility, and the belief that every family wants their child to succeed, which strengthens both achievement and the school community.

topics.title: Deep Dive: T-TESS — The Texas Teacher Evaluation

blocks.text: The Texas Teacher Evaluation and Support System, or T-TESS, is the state's primary appraisal framework, designed to support continuous teacher growth rather than to function as a one-time judgment. T-TESS is built around four domains: Planning, Instruction, Learning Environment, and Professional Practices and Responsibilities. Its cycle is developmental, including a goal-setting and professional development plan at the start, ongoing observations with evidence, and a self-assessment, framing appraisal as a reflective, year-long process. A defining feature is the post-observation conference, where the appraiser and teacher discuss evidence and the teacher reflects on practice; T-TESS emphasizes teacher self-reflection and the use of student data and growth as part of evaluation. The rubric describes performance along a continuum from Improvement Needed through Developing, Proficient, Accomplished, to Distinguished, with the expectation that teachers continually move toward higher levels. The purpose is formative and supportive, identifying strengths and growth areas and linking them to professional development, rather than simply ranking teachers. On the PPR exam, strong answers treat evaluation as an opportunity for reflective growth, welcome feedback, set goals tied to student learning, and engage in ongoing professional development. Teachers demonstrate professionalism by participating actively in the appraisal cycle, reflecting honestly on practice, and using results to improve instruction. Understanding T-TESS reinforces the broader expectation that effective educators are lifelong learners committed to refining their craft.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Dyslexia & the Texas Dyslexia Handbook

blocks.text: Dyslexia is a specific learning difference, neurobiological in origin, characterized by difficulties with accurate and fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding. These difficulties typically stem from a deficit in the phonological component of language and are unexpected relative to a student's other cognitive abilities and instruction. In Texas, services are guided by the state's Dyslexia Handbook, the official framework that directs how schools identify and serve students with dyslexia. Texas law requires early screening; students are screened for risk factors, with reading instruments administered at key early grades, and teachers should watch for persistent struggles with phonemic awareness, decoding, rapid naming, and spelling. When data suggest dyslexia, schools conduct an evaluation and, if identified, provide structured literacy intervention. Effective instruction is explicit, systematic, cumulative, multisensory, and grounded in the science of reading, addressing phonological awareness, sound-symbol correspondence, syllabication, morphology, fluency, and comprehension. Students with dyslexia may receive services and accommodations under Section 504 or, where eligible, special education, and Texas requires informing families of their rights. Accommodations such as audiobooks, extended time, and assistive technology support access without lowering expectations. For the TExES, candidates connect this topic to early identification, evidence-based reading instruction, legal obligations, collaboration with specialists, and equitable support for all readers.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Response to Intervention (RTI/MTSS) in Texas

blocks.text: Response to Intervention, increasingly embedded within a broader Multi-Tiered System of Supports, is a proactive, data-driven framework for meeting students' academic and behavioral needs before difficulties become entrenched. It rests on high-quality core instruction, universal screening, ongoing progress monitoring, and increasingly intensive support matched to need. The model is typically organized in three tiers. Tier 1 is effective, differentiated instruction delivered to all students in the general classroom, expected to meet most learners' needs. Tier 2 provides targeted, supplemental small-group intervention for students who need more, layered on top of, not replacing, core instruction. Tier 3 delivers intensive, individualized intervention, often more frequent and in smaller groups, for students with significant needs. Data drive every decision: universal screening identifies students at risk, and frequent progress monitoring determines whether interventions are working and whether a student should move between tiers. MTSS broadens RTI to integrate academics, behavior, and social-emotional supports within one coherent system. Importantly, RTI is not a special education placement, though documented response data can inform an evaluation, and it must never delay a timely referral when disability is suspected. Collaboration among teachers, interventionists, and families is essential. For the TExES, candidates connect RTI/MTSS to early intervention, data-based decision-making, differentiation, and equitable access to support.

topics.title: Deep Dive: Serving Gifted & Talented Students

blocks.text: Gifted and talented students demonstrate the potential to perform at remarkably high levels of accomplishment compared with peers of the same age, experience, or environment, whether in intellectual, creative, artistic, or leadership domains or in specific academic fields. In Texas, districts are required to identify and serve these learners, and equitable identification means using multiple measures and actively seeking talent across all populations, including students who are economically disadvantaged, English learners, or twice-exceptional, those who are gifted and also have a disability. A persistent misconception is that gifted students will succeed without support; in reality, without appropriate challenge they may disengage, underachieve, or develop social-emotional difficulties. Effective service centers on appropriately advanced, complex, and depth-oriented learning rather than simply more work. Strategies include curriculum compacting to eliminate already-mastered content, acceleration, tiered assignments, open-ended and abstract tasks, independent study, and opportunities for higher-order and creative thinking. Differentiation should adjust content, process, and product to match advanced readiness and interests. Teachers must also attend to affective needs, including perfectionism, asynchronous development, and the importance of intellectual peers. Twice-exceptional learners need both enrichment and accommodation simultaneously. For the TExES, candidates connect gifted education to differentiation, equitable identification, rigorous and individualized instruction, and meeting the full range of learner needs.
